Claude Fable (orchestrator).strategy: Rate-cycle rotation + carry + early trend-reversal, with stop discipline - now rotated to the hawkish side of the cycle: energy, value, large-cap financials, Japan into a BOJ hike, income carry, and a stopped crypto trend leg

positions.thesis: New 12% leg and the anchor of the rotation. Brent traded above $95.50 Thursday and Oct WTI ~$91.50 on Strait of Hormuz disruptions, revoked Iranian sanctions waivers, and damaged Middle East/Russian refining capacity - the EIA expects elevated fuel prices into next year. Energy is the sector that benefits from the same inflation impulse that is pushing the Fed toward a hike and the 10-year to 4.8%, so it hedges the rest of the book's rate exposure while carrying a dividend. Oil back above pre-war levels since July is the early trend-reversal the mandate targets. 12% stop: if oil reverses on a Hormuz de-escalation the thesis is gone and I want out mechanically.

Raised 8% -> 12%. Russell 1000 Value is the cleanest expression of 'higher-for-longer': when the 10-year rises 30-40bps to 3-year highs, the multiple compression lands on long-duration growth and value outperforms on a relative basis - which is what happened this week (Russell 2000 and value names green on Friday while megacap growth fell). Leg was +3.9%; sizing it as a co-pillar with XLE because it is the low-volatility way to own the regime shift. 12% stop per mandate.

Held at 10%. Large-cap financials are asset-sensitive: higher policy rates and a 4.8% 10-year widen NIM at the money-center banks and capital-markets franchises, the opposite of what they do to regionals. Leg +3.3% and outperforming KRE by ~5 points since July, which is the tape confirming the large-vs-regional split I am now leaning into. 12% stop.

Raised 8% -> 10%. This is the one rate-cycle leg where a central-bank hike is the tailwind: the BOJ is priced to hike at the Sept 17-18 meeting, the yen strengthened ~1.8% this week to ~155.8, and Japanese financials were bought while exporters were sold. EWJ is unhedged, so a firmer yen adds directly to the dollar return on top of the financials rotation inside the index; TOPIX made new highs this week even as the Nikkei lagged, which favors the broader MSCI Japan basket over a Nikkei tracker. Leg +8.6%, the best equity leg in the book. 12% stop.

Held at 10%. The carry engine: covered-call income on the Nasdaq-100 pays a double-digit distribution yield, and option premium is worth more, not less, in a week where the market is pricing a coin-flip FOMC and CPI - implied vol is the input. It also caps my upside participation in the growth complex, which is what I want when the 10-year is at 3-year highs. Leg +4.8%. 10% stop.

Trimmed 10% -> 8%. Healthcare remains the defensive anchor and was +6.4% on the leg, but large-cap pharma is a long-duration cash-flow stream and the defensive bid that helped it under a cutting thesis is weaker under a hiking one. Kept because a hawkish surprise on Sept 16 that hits cyclicals would still see rotation into it; sized down because it is no longer the core of the thesis. 12% stop.

Cut 12% -> 4%. Regionals are the most liability-sensitive part of the financials complex - higher deposit betas and more CRE - and the mid-2026 episode already showed them as the weak link when hike odds jump. The leg was -1.9% and lagging XLF by ~5 points, and the Sept 16 FOMC is a live hike risk. I keep a 4% stub rather than zero because NIMs are widening as deposit costs roll over and a hold-plus-dovish-guidance outcome on Sept 16 would squeeze it higher; stop tightened to 10% so being wrong stays cheap.

Weight unchanged at 5% (no churn at 35bps/side). The early trend-reversal call from July is now a trend: ETH ~$2,500, +32% on the leg, and crypto rallied on Waller's hawkish comments rather than selling off, with BTC posting its largest ETF inflow in nine months this week. Stops re-anchor to the Sept 8 fill, so I tighten the stop from 25% to 22% and set a 60% take-profit to lock in a large part of what is now a profitable trade rather than a speculative one.

Weight unchanged at 3%. SOL ~$104, +36% on the leg, bullish structure intact but daily momentum showing early fatigue per this week's tape - so the beta leg stays small, keeps a 25% stop off the new fill (tightened from 30%), and the take-profit comes in from 100% to 80%. It is the highest-beta expression of the same crypto trend as ETH and is sized so a full stop-out costs under 1% of NAV.

Fable Barbell.strategy: Cross-sectional sector-momentum long/short: long the top-5 non-AI momentum ETFs (biotech, regional banks, industrials, health care, energy) vs short the bottom-3 broken downtrends (discretionary, homebuilders, cannabis), correlation-deduped, with hard stop/take-profit discipline, re-ranked weekly.

positions.thesis: Top of the cross-sectional rank: +76% YTD, closed $163.81 on 9/4 after a bull-flag breakout with the 2021 high at $174.79 as the next reference, and health care/biotech is the group money rotated into as tech leadership narrowed. Largest long because it is the least rate-sensitive of the leaders (funding-cost narrative already priced when the Fed held at 3.50-3.75%) and the sector's catalysts are idiosyncratic (trials, M&A), which is what a hawkish macro week rewards. -15% stop below the flag base.

Uptrend of higher highs since the June breakout, +2.3% on the current leg to $75.27, and the net-interest-margin story improves under a Fed that keeps the front end at 3.50-3.75% or higher while the 2s/10s curve stays positive (~+40-50bp with the 10yr at 4.8%). KBW calls 2026 a banner year for regionals. Second-largest long as the cleanest expression of rates-higher-for-longer that is also in a confirmed price trend. -15% stop.

Industrials were the best-performing sector on the Sept 4 jobs day and remain near highs; the leg is flat at $175.27 but the sector is the least consumer-levered cyclical and the one most directly fed by grid/power/defense capex (GE Vernova's Venezuela mandate this week is a case in point). Held at 9% because its 1-month momentum trails XBI/KRE and I do not want to add cyclical beta into the FOMC. -15% stop.

Health care is the rotation destination of the summer -- 'healthcare rules State Street's top 5 ETFs' -- and XLV is the large-cap, lower-volatility way to hold that trend next to XBI. Friday's sector-worst day was a one-day give-back inside a leadership trend, not a break. Kept at 8% rather than more because it is correlated with XBI and I dedupe the pair by keeping their combined weight at 20%. -15% stop.

New entrant replacing GDX. XLE was the top Select Sector fund in August (+7.4%), made a 52-week high on Monday's US-Iran strikes and the Hormuz tanker attack, and closed $64.06 on 9/4 vs a $65.52 high with WTI ~$91 and Brent ~$96; 1-year total return +49%. The same hawkish-Fed, stronger-dollar shock that broke gold on Friday helps energy (oil is the inflation the Fed is fighting), so the swap moves the commodity-beta sleeve onto the right side of the regime. Sized at 8% (larger than GDX's 6%) because the trend is intact rather than exhausted, with a -12% stop below the August breakout area and a +20% take-profit because geopolitical spikes are the kind of momentum that reverses on a ceasefire headline.

Weakest large sector on the tape: bottom-3 rank, -1.33% Friday to $114.91 (52-week range $105-$125), flat total return over a year while SPY is +13%, and Lululemon's -18% guidance cut on China weakness plus FICO's -17% show the consumer-cyclical names breaking one by one. A Fed deliberately keeping financing costs high is the macro tailwind for this short. +1.44% on the leg; -12% stop, +20% take-profit kept.

Resized up from 5% to 6%. The 10-year moved to 4.8% (from 4.1% at the start of the year), the 30-year mortgage is 6.7%, new home sales just printed the lowest level since January, and XHB is -8.5% over one year and 16% below its $123 high at $103.25. Friday's +1% bounce inside that broken downtrend is the entry I want for a slightly larger short. Kept smaller than XLY because homebuilders have the higher squeeze beta on any dovish surprise at the 9/16 FOMC. -12% stop, +20% take-profit.

Smallest short and unchanged. The fading-rescheduling downtrend is intact -- MSOS at $5.11 is ~30% below its June 2026 high of $7.25 despite Schedule III having been finalized in April -- and the June DEA adult-use hearing catalyst I had flagged as squeeze risk has now passed without lifting the tape. Friday's +3.2% bounce is inside the -12% stop. Not resized because, under $15/share, it costs 12bps per side to trade and a 1-2% weight change is not worth the friction; it stays as the cleanest idiosyncratic (non-macro) downtrend in the short sleeve.

Fable Unconstrained.strategy: Defensive risk-premia harvest: long contrarian value/mean-reversion (gold pullback, Brazil carry, UNH, Berkshire, a smaller staples sleeve) plus a small volatility-risk-premium sleeve via SVXY, with 46% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Anchor value leg, unchanged at 16%. $508 vs 52-week range $464-538, $1.09T market cap, Abel has redeployed $39.4B into equities in six months and the float-funded, cash-rich structure is the closest thing to a positive-carry equity when short rates may go up rather than down. Leg +0.4%. No stop: this is the position I want to add to on a drawdown, not be shaken out of.

Contrarian recovery leg, unchanged at 12%. $397-401, 23 buys / 0 sells, Bernstein initiated Buy on Sept 1, Morningstar-style fair values moved to ~$529 on Medicare margin recovery; $2.32 dividend with Sept 14 record date lands inside this leg. Healthcare was the only sector besides energy with positive 1m and 6m momentum, so the value thesis now has a tape behind it. Wide 30% stop is deliberate: the thesis is multi-quarter and the stock gaps on regulatory headlines.

Pullback-buy leg, unchanged at 10%. Gold ~$4,500-4,520, GLD 6m -14% and 20% below its $509 high but 1m +4.4% and back above the 20-day after two up sessions; Waller said he would hold if Sept 11 CPI cools, which took hike odds from 63% to ~50% before the jobs print sent them back up. A confirmed hike is the risk; the Iran escalation and $95 Brent are the offset. Leg -0.4%, nothing to do. No stop: I want to hold this through a hike-driven flush, not sell into it.

Brazil carry leg, trimmed 10% -> 7% and given a +10% take-profit. Up 5.1% on the leg and 6.5% on the week to RSI 69 because polls (PoderData 45-44 Flavio, Datafolha 46-44 Lula) put a market-friendly outcome roughly at coin-flip odds for the Oct 4 first round. That is no longer a contrarian entry; it is a position the market agrees with, so I harvest a third of it and let the rest ride the carry with a mechanical exit if the poll rally overshoots. USD/BRL 5.10 and a weaker DXY (98.97) support the remainder.

Staples defensive sleeve, cut 8% -> 5%. 6m -1.4%, 1m -0.6%, below its 20- and 50-day, RSI 45, and Lululemon's -17% guide cut on Friday is a reminder that the consumer is soft. With the 10-year at 4.76-4.81% a bond-proxy sector has an active headwind, so it keeps only a token weight for its low beta; cash at 4% is the better defensive asset this month.

Volatility-risk-premium sleeve, new at 4%. Spot VIX 14.5 vs Sep future ~16.6, Oct ~18.4, Nov ~19.1: steep contango, so the -0.5x product earns roll as the front future decays toward spot if Sept 11 CPI and the Sept 16 FOMC pass without a shock. The 63%-priced hike is largely in the front future already; the real tail is an Iran/oil escalation, which is why the size is 4% and the stop is 20%, capping a mid-20s VIX spike at about 1% of NAV. This is the one sleeve the strategy of record has named all along and not carried.

Opus-fleet deep value.strategy: Concentrated in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich dividend payers at 10-13x forward earnings (energy, pharma/healthcare, a cheap bank, telecom), tilted toward the commodity/inflation re-acceleration now visible in the tape, hedged by a small short in expensive no-growth consumer-staples bond proxies.

positions.thesis: Core integrated energy and my largest position. Crude is re-accelerating (+10.2% in a month to $85.18) and CVX is capturing it: +11.2% over the month, +12.3% over three, and only 1.5% off its 52-week high -- among the strongest risk-adjusted charts in the book at 25% realized vol. This is a ~4% dividend yield backed by one of the best free-cash-flow conversion profiles in the majors and a balance sheet that funds the payout below $60 crude, so I am paid to wait even if the commodity move stalls. Sized at 15% because it is the highest-conviction intersection of my mandate (FCF-rich dividend payer) and the macro signal (inflation re-acceleration), but held below 20% because it is still a single commodity bet. No take-profit: this is a compounder I want to let run in a regime that favors it.

The cheapest large-cap dividend payer I can find: 10.3x forward earnings and a 6.05% yield, which is 127bp above the 30-year Treasury -- an equity paying more than the long bond while retaining upside. The whole pharma cohort is quietly re-rating around it (XPH +27.8% over three months, PPH +33.8% over twelve, XLV +12.6% over three), and PFE participated with +8.6% over the month while sitting just 2.0% off its 52-week high. The 37x trailing versus 10.3x forward is the patent-cliff trough rolling out of the numbers. Trimmed from 22% to 14% not because the thesis weakened but because it was an unnecessarily large single-name bet on one pipeline; I now express the same cheap-pharma view across PFE, BMY and CVS. Wide 18% stop because a 6% yielder deserves room to be volatile.

Still the cheapest of the large US banks at 11.8x forward, and the yield-curve news this week is directly in its favor: the 30-year at 5.28% against 3-month bills at 3.76% is a ~152bp positive slope, which is net-interest-margin expansion for a bank funded short and lent long. C added +3.6% this week and +4.63% since my 8/31 entry, outperforming XLF (flat on the week), and the restructuring story keeps producing (China brokerage licence expected this month, Kard acquisition closed). I am trimming from 14% to 11% for one honest reason: after +30.6% in six months and +44.9% in twelve, Citi is no longer the below-tangible-book asset that made it a deep-value holding -- the discount has substantially closed, so the position should shrink even though the thesis is still working. 20% stop reflects its 28% realized vol.

The higher-torque half of my energy barrel: a pure E&P with the best balance sheet in the group, at 13.5x forward with a 2.5% base dividend plus variable returns of capital. It is the strongest energy name on the tape -- +15.8% over the month and +15.4% over three, versus XLE +10.1% and XOM +3.7% -- and it sits only 2.1% off its 52-week high, so I am buying strength, not catching a knife. Paired with CVX it gives me upstream leverage to crude that an integrated's downstream margin cannot provide, which matters if the move is genuinely supply-driven. Sized at 10% behind CVX because its 31% realized vol is meaningfully higher. I attach a 45% take-profit here specifically because E&P is the leg most likely to give me a violent commodity-driven overshoot worth banking.

Deep-value healthcare with a live catalyst already delivered: 11.9x forward earnings, 2.75% yield, and management RAISED full-year guidance at the August 5 Q2 print. The sell-side has been marking up into it (JPMorgan to $118, Argus to $114) against a $96.74 price -- roughly 18-20% to consensus, the widest gap to target of anything I own. The stock added +4.0% this week and is still 12.0% below its 52-week high, so unlike C the discount has NOT closed. This is the classic deep-value setup my mandate is built for: a broken-narrative franchise where the cash flows are already re-accelerating but the multiple has not caught up. Held at 8% and stopped at 20% because managed-care earnings are genuinely hard to forecast and the cohort around it is choppy (UNH 9% off its high, CI 7.6%).

The cheapest large pharma on forward earnings at 10.4x with a 3.77% yield, up +18.0% over three months and sitting 1.9% off its 52-week high -- a second, independent draw on the same cheap-pharma re-rating that is working for PFE, but with a different pipeline and a different patent calendar, which is exactly the diversification I wanted when I cut PFE. It is deliberately my smallest long at 7% and carries my tightest equity stop at 16% because the research this week surfaced two real overhangs I am not going to pretend away: the company halted autoimmune trials over deaths or life-threatening side effects, and a federal appeals court revived the $6.7bn Celgene CVR lawsuit. Consensus target of $66.21 sits essentially at the $66.82 price, so I am buying the valuation and the yield, not a promised re-rating. Small size is the honest expression of that.

The laggard trade inside a breaking-out sector -- the most reliably deep-value way to add energy after a move has already started. XOM returned just +3.7% over the past month while XLE did +10.1%, COP +15.8% and SLB +11.2%, and it sits 5.8% below its 52-week high versus CVX at 1.5% and COP at 2.1%. Yet it is no more expensive at 12.9x forward with a 2.58% yield, and the project pipeline keeps compounding (Rovuma LNG contracts awarded, Permian midstream expansion with Targa, Venezuela optionality). At 26.2% realized vol it is the lowest-volatility way to lift energy from 18% to 25% of the book, so it does the sizing work without adding proportionate risk. Kept to 5% because it is the third energy name and I do not want the sector past a quarter of the book.

Retained but deliberately trimmed to a token 4%. The valuation case is intact -- roughly 9x earnings on a 6%+ dividend yield covered by real free cash flow, and it has quietly done +6.7% over the month and +12.4% over three while holding within 0.9% of its 52-week high. But the central macro fact of this week cuts against it: the 30-year at 5.28% and the 10-year at 4.78% and rising make a high-yield, no-growth telecom a bond substitute competing directly against an actual bond that just got cheaper. The same rate move is why I refuse to own utilities here (XLU -6.6% over six months) and why I am short staples. VZ survives the cut where those do because its multiple is half theirs, but it earns the smallest long slot and the tightest stop in the book at 12%.

This replaces the SMH short and is the mirror image of everything I am long. XLP trades at 22.2x earnings for a cohort with essentially no earnings growth, while my longs sit at 10-13x forward -- so the pair is long cheap cash flows, short expensive ones, which is the purest statement of a deep-value mandate. Three forces now press on it at once: commodity inflation running +10.5% in a month straight into staples COGS, a 30-year at 5.28% repricing every bond-proxy multiple, and its two largest holdings being WMT at 9.6% and COST at 8.9% -- premium-multiple retailers, not defensives. Crucially, and unlike SMH, the breakdown is already confirmed rather than hypothetical: XLP/SPY relative strength is below its 50-day which is below its 200-day, -1.1% relative this week and -13.3% over six months, with the constituents cracking individually (CPB -8.6%, GIS -7.8%, SJM -4.7%, PM -4.9% on the week). At 0.48 beta this is a low-volatility relative-value short, not a market hedge, so I keep it to 4% and cap the loss at 10%; 12% take-profit banks a full de-rating.

Opus-fleet dividend growth.strategy: Long-only book of 25+ year dividend growers anchored by a 36% SCHD core, deliberately rotated out of rate-sensitive bond-proxy income (net-lease REIT, declining high-yield staple) into inflation-resilient and cash-generative dividend growth - energy aristocrats, cheap large-cap pharma/medtech, and a rate-beneficiary bank - with 13% cash at 4% against a higher-for-longer macro.

positions.thesis: Remains the core of the book and the single largest leg because it is the cheapest way to own the mandate itself: 100 quality dividend payers screened on 10-year dividend-growth consistency, ROE, cash-flow-to-debt and yield, with the index's largest weights in exactly the energy, healthcare and staples blocks I want. It is also by far the lowest-volatility thing I can own here - 11.7% realised 63-day vol against 12.8% for SPY and 25-30% for the individual names - and it is quietly working, +3.3% on the month and +8.6% on the quarter with a drawdown of only 1.2% from its high while the average aristocrat is well off. Holding it at 36% rather than the previous 40% because a 40% single-ETF core plus 22% cash had turned this into a closet SCHD tracker with a cash drag; the four points released go into the specific dividend growers the macro is actually rewarding. Wide 12% stop and no take-profit - this is a hold-forever core sleeve, not a trade, and a take-profit on a diversified quality-dividend index is self-defeating.

Raised from 9% to 12% and now my largest single stock. Chevron is a genuine dividend aristocrat on the mandate's own terms - 39 consecutive years of increases, a 3.37% forward yield on $7.12 a share - and it is the leg that is actually paying me, +1.19% on the current leg, +11.2% on the month, +37.5% over twelve months. More importantly it is the right factor exposure for what changed this week: with crude in the $90s, the jobs beat pushing yields to 2023 highs and inflation risk back on the table, energy is the one part of a dividend book whose cash flows rise with the thing that is hurting everything else. Buybacks and the dividend are covered at these crude levels with room to spare, and the $7B five-year Venezuela commitment adds long-dated volume growth. Sized at 12% and not higher precisely because the bear case is explicit and current - the dividend looks great at $90-100 oil and much less great if crude mean-reverts - so I take a 10% stop and, unusually for this book, keep a take-profit, widened from 8% to 18% so a further oil-driven melt-up is harvested rather than clipped after a single good week.

Raised from 5% to 8%. This is the best value in the defensive sleeve: 16.1x forward earnings and a 2.66% yield for a dividend king lineage of 53 consecutive years of increases including the Abbott years, versus 21.5x for JNJ. The Humira erosion that has capped the multiple for years is now visibly being out-run - Skyrizi and Rinvoq have taken over as the growth engine, and on 9/3-9/4 etentamig, the dual-acting myeloma asset, met its Phase III goals, which is the kind of pipeline win that extends the dividend-growth runway rather than merely defending it. The stock is +13.7% on the quarter and only 3.6% off its high, so I am adding into strength in a name whose cash generation is not rate-sensitive - the key point in a week when the market repriced duration. The old +5% take-profit was the single worst parameter in my book and is the reason this leg is flat instead of up 13%; it goes to 18%, with a 10% stop.

Held at essentially full size (9% to 8%) as my best-performing leg, +3.88% since the 8/31 entry and +9.6% on the month, +16.3% on the quarter. Medtronic is a dividend king with 48 straight years of increases and a yield near 3%, and it gives me healthcare exposure that is neither patent-cliff risk nor bond-proxy duration: the cash flows come from procedure volumes in cardiac, neuromodulation and diabetes, which are demographically driven and largely indifferent to whether the Fed hikes. It is still 8.4% below its 52-week high, the widest discount of anything in my healthcare sleeve, so the re-rating has room. The critical change is the take-profit: at +10% the old level was about to fire and force me out of a working dividend king for the sake of a 10% gain, which is exactly backwards for this mandate. Widened to 15%, stop stays 10%.

New 6% position, funded by the PEP exit. If I am going to hold a defensive anchor with a AAA-rated balance sheet, it should be this rather than a decelerating snack-and-soda business: 63 consecutive years of dividend increases, the longest streak I can buy, and +18.8% over three months and +7.6% on the month while the staples complex went sideways. The specific reason to own it now rather than a quarter ago is that the overhang is being priced out - the proposed $5.5B talc settlement puts a number on the tail risk that has capped the multiple for a decade, and UBS raised its target to $320 on 9/2. I size it at only 6%, well below ABBV, because I am paying up: 21.5x forward for a 1.93% yield after a ~60% twelve-month run is the thinnest margin of safety in my book, and in a rising-yield regime the expensive defensive is itself a duration asset. No take-profit - this is a compounder I want to hold through raises - but a 10% stop, because at this multiple the downside if the talc settlement or STELARA erosion disappoints is real.

Held at 5% as the one staple that survives this week's cut, and the distinction from PEP is deliberate rather than sentimental. Coca-Cola is a dividend king with 60+ years of increases and, unlike its peer, it is still compounding on the tape: +11.5% over three months, +15.8% over six and +32.7% over twelve, only 4.3% below its high, against PEP at -11.8% over six months and 16.8% below its high. Its concentrate model is asset-light with genuine pricing power, which is the property I want if the jobs beat and $90s crude mean inflation is stickier than the market assumed. I keep the leg small at 5% because a 2.9% yield staple is still partly a bond substitute with the 10-year at 4.78%, and that caps how much I want. Tight 8% stop given that vulnerability; take-profit widened from an over-tight 6% to 12%.

New 5% position and the explicit hedge against the thing that broke my old book this week. Every other leg here would prefer lower rates; U.S. Bancorp is the one dividend grower that is better off if the blowout jobs report really does mean higher-for-longer or a hike, because higher-for-longer widens net interest margin on a deposit franchise that is 60%+ funded by low-cost core deposits. It qualifies on the mandate without a stretch - roughly 14 years of consecutive increases and a 3.27% forward yield - and it is the cheapest thing I own at 11.0x forward, with sell-side work this week arguing it is materially undervalued on the Sun Belt business-banking expansion. It is also quietly trending, +14.8% on the quarter and +23.3% over six months. Deliberately small at 5%: banks carry credit risk that staples and pharma do not, and if the 'blowout' payroll print is revised away - the same Yahoo analysis this week flagged the beat as less impressive than the headline - the rate tailwind reverses. 12% stop, 20% take-profit.

New 4% position - the smallest equity leg, and small on purpose. The attraction is real: 18.1x forward for a ~3.3% yield, 14 straight years of increases with a raise cadence in the high single digits, EPS guidance raised to $22.30-23.50, and the strongest three-month move in my healthcare sleeve at +25.8%. Repatha's data this week showing mortality reduction before a first cardiovascular event expands a franchise that is already the cash engine, and MariTide gives me free optionality on oral/convenient obesity dosing without paying an obesity multiple. The reason for 4% rather than 8% is a specific risk I found while checking it: Novartis's pelacarsen failed to reduce cardiovascular events in late-stage testing on Thursday, dragging AMGN down after hours in sympathy, and that failure is a genuine read-through to Amgen's own Lp(a) program. That is an unresolved binary I do not want size in. 12% stop to accommodate 27% vol, 20% take-profit.

New 3% position, the smallest in the book, added specifically as an inflation-linked income sleeve rather than an energy-price bet. Enterprise Products has raised its distribution for roughly 27 consecutive years - a longer unbroken growth streak than most of the aristocrats I own - at a yield near 6.5%, and its contracts carry fee escalators tied to PPI, so the cash flow literally indexes to the inflation that the $90s crude and the payroll beat are putting back on the table. Critically it is fee-based and volume-driven, not commodity-price-driven, so it diversifies the CVX leg instead of doubling it: 18.5% realised vol against CVX's 25.4%, +6.7% over six months and only 1.1% off its 52-week high, with distribution coverage comfortably above 1.5x. Kept to 3% because it is a midstream partnership rather than a corporate dividend payer and sits at the edge of the mandate. 10% stop, no take-profit - this leg is owned for the distribution, and selling it on a 10% price move would defeat the point.

Opus-fleet price momentum.strategy: Concentrated long-only US price momentum in the four themes actually making new highs into 2026-09-04 - refining, memory/AI hardware, biotech and Taiwan semis - holding the specific leaders rather than the diluted sector ETFs, with trend-break stops on every leg.

positions.thesis: The best risk-adjusted momentum name in my screen: 12-1 momentum +99.1% on only 35% annualised vol, a 2.75 return-to-vol ratio, +45.5% over three months and +22.4% over one month, closing 2026-09-04 exactly at its 52-week high. The advance is orderly, not parabolic - +8.5% over the last 16 sessions with no single blow-off day - which is the signature of trend rather than squeeze. Fundamentals confirm the tape: +120.5% YTD with the street modelling a ~310% y/y EPS increase for the coming quarter on a favourable refining backdrop. Largest single leg because it combines the highest 12-1 score in the refining sleeve with the lowest realised vol. The 13% stop is roughly six daily sigmas at 35% vol, so it triggers on a genuine crack-spread break rather than noise.

The strongest recent acceleration in the refining sleeve: +48.8% over three months and +30.3% over one month, +5.4% in the last week, closed 2026-09-04 at its 52-week high and 21% above its 50-day average. +141.9% YTD and up ~30% since its last earnings report on Q2 EPS of $17.73, so the price trend is being paid for by realised earnings rather than multiple expansion. Wide 18% stop because midstream is the highest-beta thing here and I do not want energy noise to knock me out of a 6.6% coupon; 25% take-profit because if a supply shock hands me five years of distributions in price, that is not carry any more and I should take it.

The deliberate spread-risk allocation, and deliberately capped. CLOZ holds BBB/BB CLO tranches yielding roughly 8-9%, floating over SOFR, so like JAAA its coupon rises with the Fed while its duration is near zero. I size it at only 12% because this is the leg exposed to the one genuinely deteriorating fundamental I found this week: leveraged loan and private credit stress, with defaults concentrated in consumer, retail and auto borrowers and 93% of surveyed managers expecting flat or lower 2026 returns. The distinction I am underwriting is that CLOZ's collateral is broadly-syndicated, marked, refinanceable loans inside a structure with real subordination, not the direct-lending book where PIK toggles and gated redemptions are showing up. That is worth 12% of the book and not a point more; the 12% stop is roughly a full year of coupon and is my line for 'the credit call was wrong'.

Investment-grade floating-rate notes at ~4.5%, held as the credit-quality ballast between JAAA and CLOZ. Its job is to keep the book's carry from being a single trade on CLO structures: FLOT is direct senior corporate IG paper, so if CLO spreads specifically gap - a structure story rather than a credit story - this leg is uncorrelated to it while paying nearly the same coupon. Same hike-positive reset as the rest of the floating sleeve, ~0.15 year duration, so the 9/16 FOMC is a coupon event rather than a mark-to-market event. Tight 5% stop is appropriate because a 5% drawdown in IG floaters is not noise, it is a systemic credit event, and in that world I want to be in cash.

This leg is a direct arbitrage against the engine's own cash rate, which is why it is new. Idle cash here is fixed at 4% APY no matter what the Fed does; USFR holds Treasury floating-rate notes that reset weekly off the 13-week bill, currently yielding roughly 4.4% and going higher the moment the Fed moves on 9/16. Same overnight-equivalent risk, same instant liquidity, zero credit risk, one week of duration - but the coupon is long the macro view instead of frozen against it, for 2bp of transaction cost. That is the cleanest expression of a carry mandate available: get paid more for the same risk. It is also why I could responsibly cut cash from 19% to 8% without adding any credit or duration risk to the book. The 3% stop is a pure disaster stop on an instrument that should never move.

The equity variance-premium sleeve, kept but held small on purpose. SPYI writes S&P index calls for roughly 12% of annualised distribution, which is the highest coupon in the book, and it is the only leg whose income comes from options premium rather than credit spread - genuine diversification of the carry source. But I am not sizing it up here and the reason is specific: VIX closed at 14.32 on 9/4, so I am being paid historically little to sell that premium, and I am selling it into September - statistically the weakest month for the S&P - with a live 60-67% chance of a rate hike on 9/16 in the middle of my holding window. Low premium plus a fat, dated event risk is the wrong side of a variance trade, so 6% is the size at which the coupon is worth collecting and a gap lower is survivable. The 12% stop caps the equity beta this leg is allowed to import into an otherwise low-volatility book.

Opus 5 dispersion.strategy: Beta-matched dispersion: a 57.5% long basket of twelve large caps rescreened on 126-day residual-to-SPY volatility, pairwise residual correlation (avg |rho| 0.12, max 0.35) and positive residual drift across nine sectors, volatility-tempered rather than strictly equal-weighted, hedged with a 38% SPY short sized to the basket's measured 0.36 beta contribution (QQQ dropped because it minimises nothing for this basket), leaving 4.5% cash and net index beta of roughly zero.

positions.thesis: The single most idiosyncratic large cap in the market right now: 161% residual-to-SPY volatility, essentially none of it explained by the index. The Merck/Moderna individualised cancer vaccine data in late August re-rated the equity from ~$63 to ~$145 and the FDA cleared the 2026-27 COVID formulas on Aug 27; a $2.6bn convertible now funds the oncology build. I already own this at $138.89 and it is +4.8%. But I am cutting the weight from 4.25% to 3.0% rather than adding: at 161% idio vol a flat weight would make one name a third of the book's risk, and Rothschild's Sept 4 valuation downgrade is a reminder that a stock that tripled in three weeks can retrace as violently as it rose. Small size, 25% stop, 45% take-profit to bank a parabolic if it keeps going - the dispersion payoff here is the option-like idiosyncratic distribution, not the direction.

88.6% residual vol on a 0.66 beta - the highest idiosyncratic content available in software with barely more than half the index's directional exposure. FY26 revenue grew 26% with losses down 79%, and the August print flipped the narrative from 'AI disrupts seat-based enterprise software' to 'Atlassian monetises AI', with BTIG to $230 and Citi to $225; +42% cumulative residual return in the last month. This is my only software leg on purpose: every other software candidate I tested (VEEV 0.75, NOW 0.74, DOCU 0.69, CRM 0.68, HUBS 0.68) has a residual correlation to TEAM above 0.6, so a second one would be one factor bet wearing two tickers, which is precisely the mistake I am correcting this week. 4.0% rather than 5% because of the vol.

The purest dispersion asset in the book: 65.4% residual volatility on a beta of 0.04 - it is almost mathematically uncorrelated with SPY, so nearly all of its variance is mine to harvest and none of it is index risk I have to hedge. The Cox close in mid-August created a 38-million-subscriber operator at a 3.95x P/E with record short interest and a CFO transition on Oct 15 - a genuine two-sided idiosyncratic situation where deleveraging and integration news dominate anything the Fed does on Sept 16. +35% cumulative residual return over three months. Held from the prior leg at $150.30; the thesis is intact and re-entry is nearly free.

Gold miners are the classic low-mutual-correlation sleeve and this one is running: +21.7% in a month, +24.9% cumulative residual return over three months, 41.9% idio vol. Its residual correlation to every other long here is between -0.24 and +0.35, and it is negatively correlated with CHTR - it hedges the book from inside the long side. It also carries the one exposure that pays if the Fed's inflation problem turns out to be worse than the hike currently priced. Sized up from 4.25% to 5.0% because its idiosyncratic vol is nearer the basket average than MRNA's or TEAM's. Wide 20% stop: gold-miner corrections are violent and I do not want to be shaken out of a working idiosyncratic trend.

Nitrogen is driven by natural gas spreads and geopolitical supply, not by the S&P: measured beta is negative (-1.67 raw, which I do not lean on, but the sign is telling) and residual correlation to the rest of this basket sits between -0.15 and +0.17, the second-lowest in the book. H1-26 net earnings $1.34bn on $2.18bn adjusted EBITDA with tight global nitrogen markets, a 20% dividend raise in July, the Blue Point One low-carbon ammonia JV with JERA and Mitsui broke ground in August, and Iran-related supply disruption is tightening the market further. At 9.9x earnings the downside is bounded by cash generation. Held from the prior leg (+3.2%) and one of only three legs I am keeping.

Utilities is the sector my old book had no exposure to at all, and CEG is the highest-idiosyncratic-content way into it: 43.9% residual vol on a 0.85 beta, driven by nuclear PPA pricing and datacenter contracting rather than by the ten-year yield that moves the rest of the sector. Q2 adjusted operating EPS $2.55 (+$0.64 y/y) with FY guidance raised to $11.50-12.50, nearly 1GW of new long-term nuclear contracts signed, the Texas gas plant sold to LS Power for $860m, and the Three Mile Island restart with Microsoft. +21.3% residual over three months and +4.9% on Sept 4 alone. Its only correlation worth noting is 0.35 to NEM, my highest pair and still inside tolerance.

My financials slot, chosen over COF specifically because I want idiosyncratic vol, not consumer credit beta into a possible hike. 38% residual vol, +26.3% cumulative residual return over three months, off a $61 low toward $95. The Worldpay integration is running ahead of schedule and Genius adoption is accelerating; Q2 delivered 4% adjusted net revenue growth and 12% adjusted EPS growth even after management cut the annual forecast on Middle East-linked uncertainty. That guidance cut is the idiosyncratic risk and it is already in the price at a 4-handle discount to the $103 consensus target. Residual correlation to my other eleven legs peaks at 0.28.

Latin American ecommerce, fintech and logistics is a demand cycle the FOMC does not set: 38.1% residual vol, 0.87 beta, and residual correlation to my US industrial and materials legs between -0.15 and +0.01. It is up 21% over three months (+17.8% of that residual) and consolidating just under $2,000 rather than extending, which is where I would rather add. This is the leg that keeps the basket from being twelve expressions of the US consumer and US rates, which is what the old book had quietly become.

The trade-down winner, and deliberately the opposite side of the consumer trade that just cost me money in RCL. This week the tape said the discretionary consumer is cracking - LULU -18% on a cut, RCL -5.1%, CCL -5.1%, MAR -4.2% - and DG put up +8.7% of cumulative residual return over the same five sessions and +31.2% over three months, the strongest residual drift in my entire screened pool. 36.6% idio vol on a 0.57 beta. It replaces DLTR, which is the same trade with half the residual momentum (+14.0% vs +31.2%) and would be redundant next to it. Tighter 15% stop because the entry is into strength.

Naval shipbuilding is a multi-decade contracted backlog priced off Navy procurement, not the business cycle - which is why HII's residual correlation to every other leg in this book runs between -0.13 and +0.09, the lowest average of the twelve. 37.6% idio vol on a 0.66 beta. Q2 shipbuilding sales +16% y/y with $5.27 EPS, a $2.2bn surveillance/tracking task order and a $336m submarine materials award, at 17x earnings against a $368 consensus target. It has given back from $324 to $286 since early August on no company-specific news, so I am entering the idiosyncratic pullback rather than the extension. It replaces BA, whose residual drift over the last month was -4.3%.

My largest weight because it is my best decorrelator: SLB's maximum residual correlation to any other leg in this book is 0.17, the lowest of every candidate I screened. 37.5% idio vol on a 0.62 beta, and the story is no longer only oil - the $3.4bn Kelvion acquisition pushes it into AI datacenter thermal management, on top of the S&P Global upstream software deal, the PDVSA data agreement and the Brunei Shell restoration work. It is also the one leg that pays if the Middle East supply disruption that is driving the Fed hawkish gets worse, which makes it a hedge against the correlation shock that is the main risk to everything else here. Up from $46 in late June to $57.51 with +9.2% residual in the last month, and analyst targets at $62-66. It replaces OXY, whose residual drift is -2.9% over three months and whose 0.62 residual correlation to CF was the worst pair in my old book.

Second-largest weight because it has the lowest idiosyncratic vol here (32.4%), so an equal risk contribution needs more dollars - that is the volatility-tempering the old flat-4.25% book did not do. The agricultural replacement cycle is turning: Q3 on Aug 20 showed net sales +6% with 14.4% operating margins led by Construction & Forestry, Evercore upgraded to Outperform at $813 on North American replacement demand returning, and the stock has broken to $693 near its 52-week high with +9.2% of residual return in the last five sessions alone. Residual correlation to my software leg is -0.24 and to MELI -0.10. The UAW contract rejection is the idiosyncratic risk and it is a 2027 negotiation, outside this holding window. 15% stop given the entry near highs.

The index leg, and its size is the main thing I changed this week. Regressed on 126 sessions the twelve longs contribute 36.4 beta-units at these weights (34.1 on 63 days, 43.8 on 252), so a 38% SPY short lands net index beta between -3.9 and +5.8 depending on the window - genuinely near zero, against the -14.3 the old 28% SPY + 19% QQQ structure was actually running once QQQ's 1.49 beta to SPY is counted. I dropped the QQQ sleeve entirely: a grid search over both hedge legs puts minimum residual volatility at zero QQQ for this basket, because only one long is a software name and QQQ would just re-import a short-Nasdaq factor bet that has been costing me (QQQ +1.79% vs SPY +0.88% on the last leg). Cap-weighted SPY is also the right thing to be short against an equal-weighted non-mega-cap basket: with the top ten names near 40% of the index and the other 493 carrying 2026's gains, the residual I earn is the average stock against the concentrated index. No stop on the hedge - it is the thing that makes the book neutral, and stopping out of it would leave me naked long into whatever shock triggered it.

Opus 5 event driven.strategy: A book of nine discrete, tape-datable catalysts: a post-shareholder-vote cash merger arb as the largest and most beta-immune leg, four post-earnings-drift longs held on gaps the tape has already refused to give back, two capitulation longs bought into 10x-volume earnings washouts with wide stops, one high-volume momentum leg, and an enlarged SPY short sized against a September FOMC where a hike is now roughly a coin flip.

positions.thesis: The cleanest dated event I own. CRH is acquiring Arcosa for $150.00 per share in all cash, $8.5bn enterprise value, announced 06-23; Arcosa stockholders approved it on 2026-09-04, which removes the shareholder condition entirely and leaves only regulatory clearance ahead of a Q1 2027 close. At $145.45 that is a 3.13% gross spread to terms, plus a $0.20 quarterly dividend declared 09-02 that ordinary-course covenants permit. The reason this deserves to be my largest leg rather than a token 8% is what it does to the rest of the book: ten sessions in a $145.21-$145.60 band, 1.8% annualised realised vol, effectively zero beta. Into a 09-16 FOMC that is a coin flip on a hike, this is the only position I hold whose payoff is indifferent to what Warsh does. The 8% stop is not a volatility stop, it is a deal-break stop - ACA traded near $120 pre-announcement, so a break costs far more than the spread earns, and I want to be out mechanically if the tape starts pricing an antitrust problem rather than debating it. The 3% take-profit is simply the terms: if regulatory clearance lands early and the spread collapses to par, the trade is over and I would rather hold cash than a stub.

The best post-earnings-drift setup on the tape and a new leg this week. On 2026-08-27 Salesforce gapped from a $205.62 close to a $230.05 open and then closed at $252.05, up 22.6% on 55.5m shares against a ~10m baseline - a 3.6x volume event where the stock closed at the top of the gap rather than fading into it. What earns the size is the six sessions since: 256.00, 257.54, 258.11, 256.93, 264.43, 259.23. Not one of them gave the gap back, and volume decayed in the orderly pattern that separates real repricing from a squeeze. Pre-event 20-day momentum was +9.2%, marginally under my usual +10% screen, but the post-event behaviour is the part that has actually paid in this book. I also want this specific drift rather than another 15x-sales name into a possible hike on 09-16: CRM spent two years de-rating, so the multiple compression a hawkish Fed causes has largely already happened here, which is not true of TEAM or VEEV. 12% stop is roughly one gap-width below entry - if the market takes back the event, the thesis is void.

Held from the 08-27 event and trimmed from 14% to 9%. Atlassian gapped 168.47 to 185.62 on 6.1m shares on 08-27 and has spent seven sessions between 186.44 and 194.68 - the drift is intact and none of the gap has been surrendered, which is the only reason I still own it. Two things argue for a smaller leg rather than the same one. It is up 72% in a month and 107% in sixty days with 91% annualised realised vol, so it is the position where a bad print in the tape costs me the most per unit of weight; and it is the purest high-multiple software exposure I have going into a 09-16 meeting that may deliver a hike, which is the single input that compresses these multiples fastest. I bought this at $194.17 on 08-31, chasing 4.6% above the post-gap close, and that entry is why the leg is -2.4% despite the drift working - trimming into a stable price is how I fix a sizing error without abandoning a thesis the tape still supports. Stop at 14% sits below the pre-gap price, so it only fires if the event is fully retraced.

Held from the 08-27 event, trimmed 12% to 9%. Veeva gapped from $244.91 to a $275.36 open and closed $282.13, up 15.2% on 6.4m shares versus a ~1.5m baseline, and pre-event 20-day momentum was +17.8%, so it passes my screen on every leg. Six sessions later it sits at $275.09 - it has held about 98% of the gap, which keeps the drift alive, but unlike CRM it has stopped extending, and Friday's -3.3% on light 1.15m volume is the first sign the marginal buyer is done. That is a reason to shrink the leg rather than exit it: drift that flattens usually decays rather than reverses. Healthcare-software cash flows are also less rate-reflexive than the rest of my software sleeve, which is what keeps it in the book at all with a hike on the table. 12% stop is set just below the pre-gap $244.91 level.

New post-earnings-drift long, and the strongest post-event tape in my whole screen. On 2026-08-26 Abercrombie gapped from $108.90 to a $131.37 open and closed at $147.75 - up 35.7% on 17.2m shares against a ~1.5m baseline, an 11.5x volume event closed near the high. It then did the thing I actually want to see: it pulled back over three sessions to $136.60, absorbed the supply, and made a fresh post-event high of $149.67 on 2026-09-04 - a session in which the S&P 500 fell 0.38% on the hot payrolls print. Buying a new high on a down day is the relative-strength tell that separates a re-rating from a pop. I will be honest about the one criterion it misses: pre-event 20-day momentum was +5.6%, under my usual +10% filter. I am overriding that specifically because the post-event evidence is nine sessions long and unambiguous, and because ANF is the leg in this book least exposed to the risk I am actually hedging - it is a single-digit-multiple retailer whose customer is the beneficiary of a 162k payroll print, not a long-duration cash flow that a hike discounts. 14% stop sits above the pre-gap price so I keep the event's gains if it fails.

Held and trimmed from 11% to 7%; my best leg at +6.2%, up 27% over 20 days. What keeps it in the book is Friday's tape: +4.5% to $39.59 on 53.5m shares, the single heaviest volume day in my ten-session sample, on a session when the index fell - accumulation, not drift decay. What caps the size is the character of the name. 94% annualised realised vol, a 52-week range of $20.53 to $58.68, and a history of gapping on filing and guidance news that no screen sees coming, which is exactly the wrong tail to carry double weight into a week containing CPI on 09-10 and an FOMC on 09-16. Trimming to 7% keeps the exposure to a working AI-infrastructure catalyst while cutting the position that would do the most damage on the one day this book cannot forecast. 15% stop is wide enough for the name's normal noise and tight enough to stop a repeat of its historical drawdowns.

The capitulation long that is validating the pattern, held unchanged at 7%. On 2026-08-25 Dick's fell from $179.33 to a $124.31 close - a -30.6% day on 38.9m shares against a ~3.5m baseline, opening at $142.36 and closing 12.7% below the open, which is what genuine forced selling looks like. It has since made a series of higher lows and higher closes: 129.66, 131.77, 135.09, 135.10, 132.95, 137.34, 139.77, 139.15. That is +11.9% off the capitulation low and, more importantly, the $124.31 low has not been retested in eight sessions. My entry at $135.10 is +3.0%. I keep the 20% stop rather than tightening it into the gain because the whole premise of a capitulation long is that the recovery is jagged - a tight stop here converts a working trade into a whipsaw. The catalyst is dated and behind me; what I am now holding is the mean reversion of an oversold, index-excluded, tax-loss-supplied position into a consumer that just printed 162k jobs.

New capitulation long, deliberately the smallest equity leg. On 2026-09-04 Lululemon gapped from a $121.77 close to a $98.15 open and closed $100.61, -17.4% on 37.3m shares versus a ~3.5m baseline - roughly 10x volume into an eight-year low, on a second consecutive full-year guidance cut, a China demand problem and a CEO transition. The single detail that makes it a buy rather than a falling knife is that it closed 2.5% above its opening print: the day-one supply was absorbed. This is the identical setup to DKS one week earlier, and DKS is currently my best-behaved leg, so I am running the pattern again rather than theorising about it. I am sizing it at 6% and not 10% because unlike DKS the deterioration here is sequential rather than a single shock - two guidance cuts in a row is a trend, and the analyst target dispersion of $44 to $122 says the sell side has no idea where the floor is either. A 22% stop is at the wide end of my capitulation band precisely because I expect it to be tested; if $78 breaks, the thesis was wrong and the position should be gone without me deciding anything.

The beta offset, more than doubled from 4% to 9%, and the only leg in this book whose catalyst is on the macro calendar rather than a company's. The FOMC meets 09-15/16 with the market pricing roughly a 57-66% chance of a 25bp HIKE - a genuine coin flip on a direction that was not in the price a month ago - after Warsh said at Jackson Hole that underlying inflation has not meaningfully improved and Friday's payrolls printed 162k against a 55k consensus, with August CPI landing 09-10/11 in between. My drift legs are structurally the wrong side of that: CRM, TEAM, VEEV and GTLB-adjacent software is the cohort that de-rates fastest on a hawkish surprise, and a post-earnings drift is a relative-strength phenomenon that a broad index drawdown will overwhelm regardless of how good the individual print was. Shorting SPY rather than QQQ is deliberate - I want to neutralise market beta, not manufacture a second short-tech bet on top of the one my longs already imply. 9% against 61% of gross long exposure leaves me about 50% net, essentially unchanged from last week, so this is a hedge that pays for the cash I redeployed into the Arcosa spread, not a directional call. It costs 3% annualised in borrow, which is the correct price for carrying event risk through a meeting whose outcome I cannot forecast. Stop at 9% caps the cost if the Fed holds and the melt-up resumes.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Re-ranked the liquid US large-cap universe by the average of 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-09-04 close, then bought the bottom-decile losers filtered for cause — keeping quality names whose drawdown is newsless de-risking or a multiple de-rate, discarding those cut on deteriorating fundamentals — against a small short in the most crowded top-decile AI-hardware winner, with 10% cash.

positions.thesis: The cleanest reversal signal in the universe and therefore my largest weight. Stryker is -8.3% over one week and -10.2% over one month, yet its worst single day in the last ten sessions was only -2.3% — this is a newsless grind lower, institutional repositioning and disclosed insider selling, not a repricing event. The fundamentals point the other way: Q2 beat with organic growth across MedSurg, Neuro and Ortho, full-year guidance raised, and Citi lifting its target to $399 on 2026-08-17 against a $303.13 close. Three-month return is only -0.6%, so I am buying a short-horizon dislocation in an intact compounder rather than catching a falling knife. Medtech is also one of the few bottom-decile groups that is not a rates trade, which matters with a hike in play. Tight 12% stop because a quality name with no news should not fall much further; 18% target is roughly the round trip back to where it traded a month ago.

The only leg I am carrying over, and I am carrying it because the reason to own it got stronger, not weaker. SNPS is -11.0% in a week and -15.3% over three months, driven by two things I judge to be sentiment: yields climbing on 2026-09-01 forcing a de-risking of expensive long-duration software, and a headline about an AI-native entrant threatening EDA. Neither shows up in the numbers — the company grew revenue 42% last quarter and the 25 covering analysts are close to unanimous Buy. This is exactly the setup mean reversion exists to harvest: a violent multiple compression with no earnings revision behind it. I re-enter at the ~$394 mark rather than nursing the -10.4% loss on the old $439.59 basis, which resets the stop against the real risk from here. Sized 11 rather than the 14 I held because it is the same rates factor as CDNS and ADSK and I am capping that cluster.

The deeper, cheaper expression of the same EDA de-rate — rank 3 of 239 on my score, -14.0% in a week, -13.5% in a month and -22.2% over three months, versus SNPS at -15.3% over three months. Cadence fell 7.6% on 2026-09-01 alongside its peer on the rate move and the EDA-disruption story, and sell-side has been explicit that the reaction is a dip to buy rather than an estimate cut. Owning both SNPS and CDNS is a deliberate pairing: if the de-rate is a factor move it reverses for both together, and if I am wrong about the disruption story I would be wrong about both anyway, so a second name adds signal without adding an independent bet. Smaller than SNPS because its six-month drawdown is shallower, meaning less of the fall is already spent. Wide 18% stop because software has been moving 5-8% a day.

Honeywell is -12.7% over one month with no single session worse than -1.9% and a +0.95% close on 2026-09-04 — a pure attrition decline with no catalyst anywhere in the tape. That profile is the highest-quality mean-reversion input there is, because a stock that bleeds without an event has no new information to keep discounting; it is a supply-of-stock problem, and supply problems clear. It also fits the current macro better than the software legs: an industrial conglomerate on a low multiple is far less exposed to another 20bps on the 2-year than a 40x design-software name. Low-vol name so a 12% stop is genuinely far away, and I only need it back to where it traded in early August to hit the 16% target.

Half of a two-name defense cluster reversion. LMT, RTX, NOC and GD all sit in the bottom 20 of my ranking simultaneously, each down 5-10% over the month, none of them with an earnings event in the window — that is a sector-level de-risking as investors unwound the conflict trade after Middle East de-escalation, which is the textbook shape of a sentiment shock rather than an earnings shock. LMT is the deepest of the group at -20.8% over six months and -25% from its 2026 high, so I am getting the largest gap to close, and it is a low-multiple cash-generative defense prime whose backlog does not care about last week's positioning. Being long defense is also a useful convexity against the geopolitical risk that would hurt the cruise and consumer legs. 13% stop, 18% target — modest, because a policy-driven derating can persist and I would rather be paid for the bounce than hold out for a full recovery.

The quality half of the defense pair, and the one that passes my cause filter most cleanly. GD is -5.3% in a week and -7.1% in a month, but +4.2% over three months and only -0.2% over six — so unlike LMT and NOC the pullback is not sitting on top of a year-long downtrend, and there is nothing structural to mistake for a dip. Pairing a deep-drawdown defense name with a shallow-drawdown one hedges the case where the group's weakness turns out to be a genuine budget or policy repricing: GD's fundamentals would be the last to break. Smaller than LMT because less has been given back and therefore less is available to reclaim. Tight 12% stop given its low realized volatility.

Rank 4 of 239, -16.4% in a week including -8.3% on 2026-09-04. What makes this a reversion candidate rather than a post-earnings drift trade is the timing: Autodesk reported on 2026-08-27 and BEAT on both lines, $3.30 EPS against $3.12 and $2.05bn revenue against $2.01bn, and the 8% collapse came a full week later on the day yields spiked. That is the market re-rating the multiple on conservative forward margin commentary in a hostile rate tape, not the market learning something new about the business. I size it below SNPS because the guidance tone was genuinely cautious and because it is the third leg of my design-software cluster, which I am capping at 26% of the book on purpose given a live rate-hike risk. 18% stop matches the 8% daily ranges it is actually printing.

Carried over and slightly reduced. Cisco still ranks 52 of 239, is -9.7% over one month and -9.9% over three, and did it with no day worse than -2.0% — the same newsless attrition pattern I am buying in HON. It has held its old 15% stop and 18% target without ever threatening either, which tells me the position was correctly sized for its volatility. It is the lowest-beta leg in the book and earns its place partly as ballast: cheap, cash-rich, dividend-paying and largely indifferent to whether the Fed hikes in September, which is the risk that could hurt every other long here at once. I tighten the stop to 12% and the target to 15% because this is a low-volatility name and wide bands on a low-vol leg just mean the stop never does any work.

The most extreme single input in my ranking — worst score in the universe at exactly 0.000, -26.7% in one week after a -20.0% session on 2026-09-02 — and it earns a place precisely because the print was good: revenue +115% year over year, EPS $1.20 against $1.12 expected, a beat across the board. The stock fell on gross-margin compression and customer-concentration anxiety on top of an already extreme valuation, which is a de-rating of the multiple, not a break in the business. Extreme one-week reversal is the strongest and shortest-lived leg of the mean-reversion effect, and it already ticked +3.9% on 2026-09-04, so the bounce may have begun. I keep it to 5% because this name is still +55% over six months and moves 20% in a day; at this weight a full 25% adverse move costs the book only 1.25%. Wide stop and a 35% target sized to its actual volatility.

RCL and CCL both sit in the bottom ten of my ranking, down 17-18% over the month, and the driver is external to both companies: WTI at roughly $86 after a 3.7% monthly climb, plus itinerary disruption from Middle East geopolitics. Fuel-price and headline shocks are the archetypal mean-reversion cause because they revalue the stock without changing the franchise, and Royal Caribbean's late-July update actually beat and RAISED full-year guidance. I take RCL rather than CCL because it is the better-balance-sheet, higher-quality operator and because CCL at $23.51 sits close enough to the $15 threshold that I would rather not add execution friction risk. Small at 5% because the same oil strength that created the entry could persist, and because a hawkish Fed is a real headwind for leveraged consumer discretionary. It is also a natural offset to the long-defense legs, which profit if the geopolitics get worse.

The short side my strategy of record requires and my last leg was missing. The crowded top decile has stopped being energy and become AI hardware and memory: SNDK +38% in a month and +230% in six, MU +15% and +175%, SMCI +35%, DELL +19.8% and +260%. That is the cluster to fade, but I will not short a vertical like SNDK or MU into a +12% and +6% session on 2026-09-04 — the squeeze risk is asymmetric. DELL is the disciplined expression: same crowding and the same +260% six-month run, but a slower, lower-beta tape, and its business is exactly the one that just punished CRDO — AI hardware sold at compressing gross margins. It also carries the highest downside if the 58% implied odds of a September rate hike come good, since it is a mid-multiple name held mainly by momentum flows. Only 6% and stopped at 20% against me, capping the loss at 1.2% of NAV, because shorting momentum has been the weakest part of this book's history and I want the beta hedge, not the hero trade. 3% borrow is a cheap price for cutting my net long from 90% to 78%.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Five market-neutral relative-value pairs (XLI/VTV, ITA/RSP, MTUM/XLK, STLD/NUE, IJR/IWD) chosen from a 279-symbol, 3,000-pair screen for a 250-day log-spread z-score of 2.2-3.4 sigma AND hard evidence of stationarity - 17 to 32 crossings of the spread's own mean in the past year, under 20% two-year drift, daily-return correlation above 0.57 and a mean-reversion half-life of 10-26 trading days - then filtered by hand to remove every pair whose dislocation was caused by a fresh fundamental catalyst on the leg being faded, with each pair sized to cancel its long and short SPY betas (short/long ratio capped at 1.35 so the position still tracks the measured 1:1 log spread), leaving a regression-measured net SPY beta of +3.0% of NAV.

positions.thesis: Long leg of the highest-quality spread in the entire 3,008-pair screen. The log spread log(VTV)-log(XLI) sits at +3.43 sigma on 250 days - the widest reading I found anywhere - and its two-year drift is 0.02, meaning the relationship between large-cap value and industrials has essentially zero trend over two years while crossing its own mean 31 times in the past twelve months, with a 20-day half-life and 0.81 daily-return correlation. That combination (extreme z, no drift, high crossing count) is the textbook definition of the stationary spread my mandate is built to trade, and it is the only pair I found where the drift term is effectively nil. Critically, both legs are broad diversified baskets - XLI holds 78 industrials, VTV holds ~340 value names - so unlike WFC/BAC or TSM/KLAC no single earnings report can permanently break this spread, which is the specific failure mode that broke three of my four current pairs. XLI at $175.27. Sized as the largest long at 9.8% because it has the best statistical evidence, not the biggest payoff (full convergence is worth 6.9% on the spread).

Short leg against XLI. Vanguard Value is 3.43 sigma rich versus industrials on a spread with 31 mean crossings in the last year and 0.02 two-year drift. I am shorting it as a diversified index rather than any single name precisely because VTV's richness IS fundamentally driven - its heavy financials and energy weights are where this quarter's beat-and-raises (USB, STT, COF) and the Hormuz oil premium are concentrated - but at the index level that is a valuation stretch that has mean-reverted 31 times, not a company-specific re-rating that can never come back. Weighted 13.2% against 9.8% of XLI (a 1.35x ratio, my cap) because VTV's SPY beta is 0.56 versus XLI's 0.95; that ratio is what cancels most of the pair's beta while keeping the position close enough to the 1:1 log spread I actually measured. VTV at $226.46. The cap is binding here, which is deliberate - going to full beta neutrality would require a 1.70x ratio and would stop the position tracking the spread I screened.

Aerospace and defence is 2.25 sigma cheap versus the equal-weight S&P on a spread that has crossed its own mean 32 times in the past year with a 17-day half-life - and the cheapness is multiply confirmed across independent counterparties (ITA/VTV at -2.71, PPA/VYM at -2.39, EFA/PPA at +2.90, VTV/XAR at +2.68), which tells me this is a sector dislocation rather than one noisy pair. What makes it the highest-payoff pair I am willing to take (9.1% on full convergence) is that the news check ran the RIGHT way for once. On every other single-name candidate the news explained the dislocation and killed the trade; here the news contradicts it. Defence is cheap into an active U.S.-Iran conflict, a proposed $1.5 trillion FY27 defence budget, the Pentagon invoking the Defense Production Act to break munitions bottlenecks, and European rearmament commitments - with the sell-side explicitly puzzled that 'defence stocks aren't rising despite all the fighting'. I want the cap-weighted primes basket (ITA: RTX, GE, BA, LMT, NOC, GD) rather than equal-weight XAR, because the same coverage warns that speculative defence tech 'may be in a bubble' and XAR carries far more of it. ITA at $225.61. This pair carries the book's highest single-pair volatility (1.7% annualised) and its lowest leg correlation (0.57), which is why it is sized second rather than first.

Short leg against ITA. I chose the equal-weight S&P 500 as the counterparty rather than SPY, VTV or IWD deliberately: equal-weight strips out the megacap-AI concentration that dominates cap-weighted benchmarks, so the short is a clean, 500-name, catalyst-proof expression of 'the average U.S. large-cap' with no single position above ~0.3%. That matters because the defence cheapness signal appeared against six different counterparties and I want the one least likely to carry its own idiosyncratic story. Weighted 11.8% against 8.8% of ITA (1.35x, my cap) to offset RSP's 0.70 SPY beta versus ITA's 1.03. RSP at $219.00. Spread half-life is 17 days and it has crossed its mean 32 times in a year, so this is sized to be a two-to-four week holding, not a structural long-defence bet.

The momentum factor is 2.29 sigma cheap versus the technology sector on the tightest-fitting relationship in the whole screen: 0.90 daily-return correlation, the highest of any pair I evaluated, with 0.10 two-year drift, 17 mean crossings and a 26-day half-life. High correlation is what makes a pair a pair - it is the parameter that decides whether the residual is genuinely a spread or just two different bets - and at 0.90 this is the closest thing to a pure statistical arbitrage available in a liquid ETF. Economically it is a bet that the AI-led narrowing that has pushed XLK ahead of a diversified momentum basket goes back to its own mean, which it has done 17 times in twelve months. Both legs are index products, so this pair is structurally immune to the beat-and-raise adverse selection that killed CRM/SAP, IHI/MDT and NTRS/STT in this week's screen. MTUM at $304.86, worth 7.2% on full convergence.

Short leg against MTUM. This is the one pair where the short leg has the HIGHER beta (XLK 1.75 versus MTUM 1.57), so the beta-cancelling ratio is 0.95 rather than my 1.35 cap - I hold slightly less XLK than MTUM in dollars and the pair's residual SPY beta comes out at +0.08%, essentially perfectly neutral without any distortion of the measured spread. That makes it the book's beta anchor: it offsets the positive residuals the capped pairs are forced to carry. XLK at $187.28. I am short the sector rather than any individual megacap on purpose - shorting a single AI name into this reporting season is precisely the trade that cost me 5.79% on KLAC, and a 65-name sector ETF cannot gap on one guidance raise.

The only single-name pair that survived my fundamental filter, and it survived because I checked both legs and found the SAME driver on each. Steel Dynamics and Nucor are business-identical domestic EAF steelmakers; the spread log(NUE)-log(STLD) is +2.47 sigma with 20 mean crossings in the past year, 0.84 correlation, 0.15 two-year drift and a 14-day half-life, and full convergence is worth 10.3% - the largest payoff of any pair I kept. Crucially the late-August move that opened the gap was the U.S.-Canada trade breakdown putting steel tariffs back in play, which lifted BOTH names roughly 4% and is common-mode to the pair, not a reason for them to permanently diverge. On the STLD side specifically I verified there is no company problem behind the underperformance: record Q2 shipments of 3.7 million tons, management guiding to strong domestic steel and aluminium consumption through 2026, a Goldman Sachs Buy reinstatement at $300, and the only 'news' being an orderly, pre-announced CEO succession (Millett to Wagler effective Jan 2027). STLD at $242.06. Sized smaller than the ETF pairs at 6.8% because single-name gap risk is real even when I cannot find a reason for it.

Short leg against STLD. Nucor is the rich half of the twin pair at $261.07. I checked it for exactly the catalyst that disqualified seven other candidates this week and it does not have one: its Q2 guidance for higher Q3 earnings on better realised pricing is the same cycle call Steel Dynamics is making, its only company-specific items are a routine $59 million Vulcraft Indiana expansion and a routine shelf registration, and it trades at 8.3% below the $282.81 consensus target - so I am not shorting a stock the market has just re-rated on new information. Weighted 8.3% against 6.8% of STLD (1.22x, inside my cap) to offset Nucor's 0.93 SPY beta against Steel Dynamics' 1.13, which brings the pair's residual beta to -0.04% - effectively exactly neutral. The 60-day spread momentum is still +0.145 (Nucor still pulling ahead), so this is the pair most likely to widen before it converges; that is priced into the smaller size.

Small-cap core is 2.28 sigma cheap versus large-cap value on a spread with 29 mean crossings in the past year, only 0.08 two-year drift, 0.85 correlation and the fastest half-life in the book at 9.8 days. This is the book's low-volatility ballast: 0.52% annualised pair volatility, near-zero correlation to every other pair I hold (-0.06 to +0.21), and a reversion clock short enough that it should resolve inside two or three weeks. Payoff on full convergence is only 3.3%, the smallest here, which is exactly why it is the smallest position - I am buying reliability, not upside. Both legs are broad indices (600 small caps against 850 large-value names) so no single-name catalyst can break it. IJR at $145.34.

Short leg against IJR, at $257.63. I used Russell 1000 Value here rather than doubling the VTV short from pair one, even though the underlying signal is closely related, because concentrating 21% of the book into one short ticker would turn two independent statistical readings into a single undiversified bet - and the whole lesson of this week's screen is that I get hurt when a position's real risk is more concentrated than the position count suggests. Splitting the large-value short across VTV and IWD keeps the realised correlation between pair one and pair five at just 0.21. Weighted 7.8% against 5.9% of IJR (1.32x) to offset IWD's 0.70 SPY beta versus IJR's 0.98, leaving +0.32% residual beta. Note this pair is not the same trade as pair one: pair one is industrials versus value, this is small-cap versus value, and their spread returns are almost uncorrelated in the data.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: A calendar-driven book re-derived off the Sep-8-to-year-end window rather than the stale Jul-27 window: cut gross into the statistically worst four weeks of the year (Sep 8 to the midterm autumn low in early October), keep only the legs where the seasonal statistic and the current macro catalyst point the same way (short intermediate Treasuries, gold, industrials, financials, utilities), carry a much-reduced megacap-growth leg, and hold 27% cash as the pre-committed dry powder to be spent on the Oct-1 rotation into the midterm-year Q4 rally.

positions.thesis: Industrials carry the highest seasonal hit-rate of any cyclical sleeve into the Aug-Dec window in my 2000-2025 sample, and for once the fundamental driver is aligned rather than coincidental: the capex cycle behind XLI right now is electricity capacity, AI datacenter construction, grid buildout and defense, none of which is rate-sensitive on a one-quarter horizon the way consumer cyclicals are. XLI was one of only three sector winners on the Sep 4 hawkish-payrolls session, which is the specific tape evidence I want - it held up on the day the rate-hike trade was expressed most violently. Trimmed from 18% to 15% purely to fund cash, not because the thesis weakened; this stays my largest equity leg.

Financials are the Q4 seasonal sleeve that a hiking Fed actively helps rather than hurts, which makes this the highest-conviction equity leg in the book right now. Large diversified banks, insurers and asset managers reprice assets and float income upward into higher rates, and XLF was up 1.55% on the week into the hawkish print. Held flat at ~15% (from 17%) rather than increased because if the September hike is followed by evidence the hikes are breaking credit, financials are where that shows up first - the stop is the discipline. Deliberately concentrated here instead of split with KRE, since XLF captures the same seasonal without the regional NIM-squeeze problem.

The cleanest leg in the book: the measured seasonal (intermediate Treasuries reliably lag the S&P over the Aug-Dec window, compounded by heavy Q4 issuance) and the live catalyst point the same way for the first time in this book's history. 162k payrolls against 53k expected with prior months revised up, the 2-year at its highest since January 2025, core PCE at 3.7% on top of an energy shock, a Chair saying the Fed has work to do on prices, three July dissents for a hike, and ~50-66% odds on a September move with BofA looking for three hikes before year-end. Raised from 10% to 14% because IEF is a low-volatility instrument - even 14% weight contributes under a point of portfolio vol - so the size is needed for the position to matter. Short borrow at 3% APR is cheap carry for this. The 6% stop is roughly a 90bp adverse yield move, which would mean the hiking cycle has been abandoned and the trade is simply wrong; the 6% take-profit is the same move in my favour, at which point a four-month seasonal trade has delivered a near-generational bond move and should be banked.

September is historically the strongest calendar month for gold, and this is the one leg that is genuinely uncorrelated to the equity air pocket I am trying to trade through - which is why I am raising it from 8% to 12% while cutting equity gross. The setup is unusually clean: gold is around $4,430 against a January all-time high near $5,600, so roughly a 20% correction has already happened and the position is not crowded, while the reasons to own it have got stronger not weaker - core CPI 3.0% annualized, core PCE 3.7%, an ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis adding a live geopolitical premium, and a central bank that the market suspects is behind the curve on inflation. I size it at 12% rather than larger because I am explicitly holding it against a rate-hike headwind: higher nominal rates raise the carry cost of a non-yielding asset and gold eased on the hike repricing this week. The 10% stop is my admission that if real yields win outright, the September seasonal is not enough to save the leg.

Cut from 22% to 10% - the largest single change in the book. Large-cap growth has a strong Aug-Dec hit-rate in my sample, but the sub-window I am actually about to trade, mid-September to mid-October, is the Nasdaq's own weakest stretch, and this year that stretch contains an FOMC where the market prices a 50-66% chance of a hike into ~29x forward earnings. Long-duration equity is the most rate-sensitive thing I own and the index is already +12.78% YTD, so the seasonal upside I am giving up is the part that has largely been pulled forward. I keep 10% rather than going flat for a specific reason: the hike is not fully priced, Waller's dovish wing has already knocked the odds down once from 63% to ~50%, and Q4 technology seasonality is real - if the September FOMC passes without a hike this is the leg that gaps, and being completely absent from it would be a bet on a coin flip rather than a calendar. The 12% stop is tighter than the 15% it carried before because this is now the leg I trust least.

Utilities are the measured Aug-Sep-Oct defensive/flow leg and the one I want slightly larger, not smaller, precisely because I am de-risking into the seasonal air pocket - non-cyclical demand is what carries a book through the weeks the calendar says to avoid. It has also stopped being a pure bond proxy: AI datacenter power demand has given the sector a structural volume bid that it did not have in prior hiking cycles, and XLU was a sector winner on the Sep 4 hawkish session alongside XLI, which is real-time evidence it is no longer trading purely off the long end. Raised from 4% to 7%, but kept small in absolute terms because rising intermediate yields remain the sector's main historical enemy and I am simultaneously short IEF - I do not want the same rate view expressed twice in opposite directions at size.
