Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes with signals refreshed on data through the 2026-09-04 close: long where price is above both the 50- and 200-day moving average with positive 3-month momentum, short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility and then tilted toward the strongest-ranked signals, with wide catastrophe stops because weekly reassessment is the real trend-exit mechanism.

positions.thesis: The single strongest ranked signal in the equity sleeve. XLE closed at $64.06, roughly 2% below its 52-week high of $65.52, is +49.3% over one year, and posted +7.4% in August - the best of the eleven Select Sector SPDRs. Price is decisively above both the 50- and 200-day averages and 3-month momentum is strongly positive, so both filters are green. The driver is a genuine supply shock (Middle East escalation, Strait of Hormuz risk, falling US inventories) rather than multiple expansion, and the sector trades at 16.4x with a 2.37% yield, so the trend is not being carried by valuation. Sized at 17% - above its inverse-vol share at ~22% realised vol - because signal strength justifies a tilt, and it is the lower-volatility way to own the energy trend alongside USO. Wide 20% stop matches the sector's volatility and lets a normal correction breathe.

The cleanest short in the book. TLT closed at $82.21 against a 52-week range of $81.17-$92.19 and is within $1.54 of its all-time low of $80.67, so price is below both the 50- and 200-day averages with negative 3-month momentum - both filters negative, which is my short condition. The macro is pushing the same way: August payrolls printed 162k versus 55k expected, Warsh told Jackson Hole the Fed still has work to do on inflation, September hike odds jumped from 35% to ~52-58%, and the 10-year is at 4.79%, near its highest since October 2023. Short borrow costs only 3% APR (about 6bps a week on this weight), so carry is not a reason to avoid it. I sized this at 16% rather than the ~23% that pure inverse-vol would assign because a hike is barely more than a coin flip and a no-hike surprise is the one event that produces a fast adverse move; the 10% stop is deliberately tighter than my equity stops for the same reason - a 10% TLT rally would mean the rate trend has genuinely broken.

The core index trend remains intact and is the lowest-volatility way to hold beta. The S&P closed the week at 7,718.60, up 0.1% on the week and still in a record-rally regime, with price above both the 50- and 200-day averages and positive 3-month momentum. I hold the index rather than XLK specifically: XLK is +44% YTD but sits 5.9% below its high, hugging its 50-day EMA at 37x earnings while the tape shows money rotating out of tech into healthcare - a decaying signal I do not want to size into just because its trailing return is large. SPY gives me roughly 35% tech exposure inside a broader, better-behaved trend. At ~14% realised volatility it earns a large inverse-vol weight; 16% reflects a slight haircut for the fact that rising yields are a headwind to the index multiple.

My best non-commodity diversifier and the one leg from the old book whose signal strengthened rather than decayed. XLV closed at $171.45 against a 52-week high of $176.60, is +27.4% over one year, and is above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum. Crucially the flow story supports the trend continuing: healthcare has become the destination for investors rotating out of expensive tech, with Eli Lilly and J&J making new highs. At ~14% realised volatility it is a large inverse-vol weight, and it is the leg least correlated to the energy/rates factor that dominates the rest of this book, which is precisely why I keep it at full size rather than selling it to fund more oil.

Copper is at record levels and I was badly underweight it at 5%. CPER closed at $39.95 against a 52-week high of $40.97 and a low of $27.85, and is +40.9% YTD - price above both averages, 3-month momentum strongly positive. The demand side is structural rather than cyclical (AI data-centre buildout, electrification, grid expansion) and it is colliding with supply constraints and disruption in major producing regions, which is the kind of setup that produces persistent rather than mean-reverting trends. Tripling the weight to 12% reflects both the signal rank and ~28% realised volatility; the 20% stop is wide enough to survive the sharp shakeouts that base metals produce inside intact uptrends. The 0.97% expense ratio is real but small against the trend.

New leg and the most direct expression of the strongest trend in the whole cross-section: USO is +89.7% over one year at $141.96, with WTI testing $91 on Strait of Hormuz disruption risk, falling US inventories and record Labor Day gasoline prices. Owning XLE alone under-expresses this - energy equities capture a fraction of the crude move. I hold this at only 10% rather than matching XLE because it is a front-month WTI futures vehicle: ~40% realised volatility, roll drag, and a -6.39% average annual return since inception, so it is a trend-rental, never a hold. Inverse-vol sizing does most of the work here. This is the one leg where I attach a take-profit: crude supply shocks spike and then fade hard, so a 40% gain gets banked mechanically rather than surrendered, and the 25% stop respects the volatility. Combined with XLE this puts 27% in energy, which is a deliberate concentration into the trend that is actually running.

The signal genuinely flipped this month. Bitcoin closed below its 200-day moving average for 270 consecutive sessions through late July; it has now reclaimed it, trading around $81k against a 200-day average near $69.4k, after +25% in August on $3.52bn of spot-ETF inflows. Price above both the 50- and 200-day with positive 3-month momentum is my long condition, so it stays in the book. It stays small at 5% because ~50% realised volatility gives it the smallest inverse-vol share of any leg, and because the signal is a fresh reclaim rather than an established trend - it is still 9.6% below where it started the year and a hawkish Fed already knocked it below $78k intraday once after Jackson Hole. I keep the 1x perp rather than spot: at 7.5bps of notional per side plus 10% APR funding (~19bps a week) it is cheaper than 35bps-per-side spot for a book that is reassessed weekly. Leverage stays at 1 because levering the highest-volatility asset would break the risk-parity logic the whole book is built on.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Concentrated long the record US refining crack spread across four refiners (62%), on the view that the binding constraint is physically destroyed refining capacity rather than the crude price, ballasted by healthcare, partially hedged by a small airline long that pays if the crack normalises, and 18% cash into the 11 Sep CPI and 16 Sep FOMC.

positions.thesis: Largest US refiner by throughput with a Gulf Coast and Mid-Continent system weighted to distillate, which is precisely the barrel the market is short: the US diesel crack set an all-time record above $106/bbl on 1 September. This is my highest-weight leg because it is the one that has already proven itself in my book, +4.17% since the 31 August entry versus +0.32% for my 2x levered crude-beta leg over the same days, which is the empirical basis for rotating the whole energy allocation from crude price into refining margin. MPC also converts the margin into shareholder returns faster than peers through its buyback, so record cracks compound into per-share earnings rather than sitting on the balance sheet. Size raised from 20% to 22%. Stop at 14% because refiners are up over 80% YTD and a ceasefire headline is a real gap risk; take-profit at 30% rather than the previous 35% because I want to bank a cyclical peak rather than round-trip it.

The purest and most export-levered way to own the diesel crack: no upstream, no midstream ballast, so the record margin flows almost undiluted to earnings. Q2 2026 net income was $3.7bn and the stock trades at 8.7x forward earnings at $370.72, within 1.2% of its 52-week high of $375.11, while the 20-analyst consensus target of $319.63 sits 14% BELOW the market price. That gap is the trade: targets have not been marked to a $106 diesel crack, so the next revision cycle is upward and the October earnings print will be measured against numbers set before the crack doubled. Already +3.29% for me since 31 August, confirming the same signal as MPC. Held at 21% rather than pushed higher because VLO and MPC are the same factor and I want the operational diversification of four refiners rather than two. Stop 14%, take-profit 30%.

New leg. HF Sinclair captures the Mid-Continent crack, which is structurally the widest in the country because it is inland and insulated from waterborne product imports that could otherwise relieve the shortage. Q2 2026 net income was $892m against $208m a year earlier and adjusted refinery gross margin rose 57% to $25.95/bbl, on record adjusted EBITDA, at a 10.1x P/E and $105.41 a share. It carries two catalysts the large-caps do not: the announced separation of the Lubricants and Specialties segment, which surfaces value the refining multiple currently suppresses, and the Western Gateway Pipeline JV with Phillips 66 and Kinder Morgan. Sized at 10% rather than higher for one specific reason: management guided Q3 throughput to 590-620 kbd because of a planned El Dorado turnaround, so DINO monetises less of this quarter's record crack than MPC or VLO do. Wider 16% stop to accommodate its higher single-asset operational variance.

New leg, deliberately the smallest of the four and deliberately the most levered. PBF has the thinnest balance sheet and the least hedged, most operationally geared refining system in the group, which is exactly why it is trading at 6.4x earnings on $11.56 TTM EPS at $74.34 after a 175% run: every incremental dollar of crack drops through with more torque than at MPC or VLO. This is the convexity sleeve of the refining bet. The same leverage cuts the other way, which is why it gets 9% and not 20%, and why the stop is the widest in the book at 18% to avoid being shaken out by its ordinary daily volatility while still capping the loss. Note the consensus target of $67.62 is 9% below market with UBS at $84 and Goldman at $81 against a Freedom Broker downgrade to Sell, i.e. the sell-side is openly split, which is what an unpriced supply shock looks like before it is resolved.

The genuine diversifier and the reason I can carry 62% in refiners without the book being a single coin flip. Healthcare demand does not depend on the diesel crack, on Hormuz transit volumes, or on whether the Fed hikes on 16 September, and it is the sector least exposed to the oil-cost pass-through that is squeezing the rest of the market. It returned +0.53% for me since 31 August in a week the S&P fell on Friday to 7,718.60 on a hot payrolls print, which is exactly the quiet non-correlation I am paying it for. Held at 14% rather than the previous 20% because with CPI on ~11 Sep and a live FOMC on 16 Sep, cash at 4% APY is a better carry-adjusted defensive asset than an equity sector for the marginal dollar. Intentionally no stop-loss: this is ballast, and stopping out ballast on a market-wide drawdown is the precise moment it is doing its job.

A reversal of my own short, and the structural hedge on the refining core. Airlines are short the jet crack exactly as refiners are long it, so a 6% long against 62% of refiners leaves my crack exposure firmly net long but pays me back in the one scenario that breaks the book: product supply recovering and cracks normalising after a Hormuz de-escalation, which Vice President Vance flagged this week by saying Iran's ability to control the strait is 'effectively gone'. The evidence for flipping rather than merely closing is that the short failed in its ideal conditions: with crude +8.8% on the week and the jet crack at records, JETS rose 1.05% against me, meaning the fuel-cost bear case is fully discounted and the short side is crowded. Standalone the long is defensible too: 162k August payrolls and 4.1% unemployment support travel demand, and the consolidated US carriers are pushing fares through. Sized at 6% because it is insurance, not a view. Stop 14% covers the case where airlines are hit by high fuel and softening demand at once.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Regime reclassified from calm-carry to a compressed-implied / rising-macro-risk vol floor: with VIX 14.53 at the 6th percentile of two years, VVIX 84.4 at the 1.2nd percentile, SPY 20d realized 8.1% at the 7th percentile, but 5y and 10y yields at two-year highs and a coin-flip Fed HIKE at the Sept 15-16 FOMC, the book stops harvesting carry and instead owns cheap convexity (14% VIXY), rotates its equity risk out of rate-sensitive low-vol proxies into real assets and low-duration value where volatility is actually being realized and paid, and holds 25% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: The core regime expression, upsized from 9% to 14%. VIX at 14.53 is the 6.2nd percentile of two years and VVIX at 84.42 is the 1.2nd percentile, so both spot vol and the convexity of vol are at two-year floors, while CPI, PPI and a September 15-16 FOMC carrying roughly 50-58% odds of an actual rate hike all fall within six or seven sessions of the 2026-09-08 entry. The carry cost is real and I am paying it knowingly: VIXY is -12.95% over the last month on contango, roughly 1.2% a week, so 14% of the book bleeds about 17bps a week if nothing happens. Against that, a hawkish surprise that takes VIX from 14.5 to the mid-20s is historically worth +45% or more on VIXY, which is +6.3% at the book level - a payoff-to-carry ratio I do not get to buy when VIX is at 20. The 45% take-profit is deliberately set below the 60% I used last week because the likely shock here is a hawkish repricing rather than a crash, and I would rather actually monetise a move to VIX 24 than hold out for a move to 30. The 28% stop is not a risk stop but a regime stop: VIXY would need VIX pinned near 11 for it to fire, which would mean my classification of a mispriced floor was simply wrong and I should stop paying for the option.

Doubled from 6% to 12%, and the largest non-vol leg. Broad commodities are where volatility is genuinely being realized and paid rather than suppressed: COMT's 20-day realized vol is 18.69%, the 62nd percentile of two years, against SPY at the 7th, and it has returned +10.75% over the past month and +4.32% in the last week alone while the index went nowhere. It is also the internally consistent hedge for my macro read - the Fed is contemplating a hike because PCE is 3.7%, so the asset that pays if the inflation impulse is real is the same asset that pays if the Fed is judged behind the curve. Unlike my former low-vol equity sleeve, a commodity futures basket has no duration, so a further backup in the long end that is now at a two-year high does not hurt it. The 14% stop gives a trending, high-realized-vol asset room to breathe without letting a commodity reversal, which is the main way this leg fails, run to a book-level loss.

This is the replacement for the 48% that sat in RSP and USMV, and the swap is specifically a duration swap. Minimum-volatility and equal-weight equity carry bond-proxy sensitivity that is a direct headwind with the 5y at 4.55% and 10y at 4.78%, both at two-year highs and a live hike two weeks out. Value is the low-duration equity factor: its cash flows are front-loaded, so it de-rates least when the discount rate rises, and the tape agrees - VLUE is +4.75% over a month, +7.46% over three and +43.28% over six months, against USMV +0.80%, +5.73% and +5.05%. Critically for a vol-regime mandate, it delivers that with 20-day realized vol of 12.43%, only the 21.6th percentile of its own two-year range, so I am buying the leadership factor without buying its historically expensive volatility. Sized at 13% as the single largest equity leg. The 12% stop is tight because the way this leg is wrong is a growth-scare rotation back into duration, and I want to be told quickly.

Kept as the core beta anchor but trimmed from 14% to 12%, and the stop tightened hard from 18% to 10%. I do not want to be absent from the market - the index has ground higher all round and shorting a 6th-percentile vol tape is a directional bet I am not making. But I also refuse to hold a large index position whose implied vol says a coin-flip Fed hike is a non-event. Twelve percent is the size at which SPY funds my participation without the book's outcome depending on it. The 10% stop matters more than the weight: with SPY 20-day realized vol at 8.10%, the 7.5th percentile of two years, a 10% drawdown from the entry fill is a genuine multi-sigma regime break rather than noise, so this stop cannot be shaken out by ordinary chop but will take my index beta to zero precisely in the scenario where the VIXY leg is paying and I want the cash.

Increased from 6% to 9% as the equity-form expression of the same inflation-vol read as COMT, held alongside it rather than instead of it because energy equities and a commodity futures basket fail differently - one on equity multiples, one on the futures curve. This is currently the highest-realized-vol broad sector I hold at 21.31% 20-day, the 58th percentile of two years, against an index at the 7th, which is the dispersion the regime is offering: index vol at the floor while sector vol sits mid-range. XLE is +10.14% over a month and +2.20% in the last week, so I am adding to something the tape is already rewarding, and it is one of the few sectors that is a net beneficiary rather than a victim of a higher-for-longer rate path. The 16% stop is wider than my equity legs and narrower than COMT's, matching its realized vol.

New leg, and the defensive allocation that replaces USMV without importing USMV's rate sensitivity. Healthcare is non-cyclical but not a bond proxy, so it defends against the growth-scare branch of a Fed mistake without being hurt by the yield backup that is the other branch. It also fits the mandate on its own terms: XLV's 20-day realized vol is 18.93%, the 81.7th percentile of its two-year range, one of the highest-percentile readings in my entire screen, at a time when the index sits at the 7th - if I want the dispersion in this regime I have to own the sectors where volatility is genuinely elevated, and this is one of the few defensive ones. Momentum supports it too, +4.26% over a month and +12.55% over three. Sized at 8% and stopped at 14%, wide enough for its realized vol.

The smallest and most volatile leg, held for convexity per dollar rather than for size. GDX's 20-day realized vol is 51.16%, roughly six times SPY's 8.10%, so 7% of the book here contributes more variance than 20% in an index fund - which is the point in a regime where I want vol exposure but cheap ones are scarce. It is up 18.28% in a month and 25.90% in three. I am explicit that this is the leg most exposed to being wrong: a Fed that hikes and is believed lifts real yields and normally hurts gold. What makes me hold it anyway is that the miners produced that +18% move while the 5y and 10y were climbing to two-year highs, which says the bid is an inflation-credibility bid rather than a rate bid, and that is precisely the scenario a 3.7% PCE print with a hesitant Fed creates. The 40% take-profit exists because this is a leg to harvest, not to marry, and the 22% stop is sized to its own volatility so an ordinary miner drawdown does not close it.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening expressed outside the US index-structure trade: long international developed and emerging markets, the physical AI/defense capex complex, large-cap value, insurance and power, funded against a short of the crowded US momentum factor.

positions.thesis: The largest leg, and the most literal reading of the mandate: broadening does not stop at the US border. Developed ex-US equity is the deepest pool of the market that is not the Mag 7 - Europe and Japan large-caps trade at a persistent multiple discount with far less index concentration than the S&P, so a world where leadership disperses is a world where they re-rate. The honest risk is the dollar, which firmed on Friday's hawkish reset and would firm further on a September hike, translating foreign returns down; that is why this is 13% rather than 20% and why it carries a 12% stop. I take that risk because dollar strength driven by US rate differentials tends to be the thing that mean-reverts once the hike is actually delivered.

The physical AI trade rather than the software AI trade, at $55.16 after a 21% trailing year. Everything the market is paying enormous multiples for in semis and software has to be poured, wired and energized first: grid capacity, transmission, datacenter construction, electrical equipment, engineering and construction. Industrials were one of only three winning sectors on Friday's hawkish tape and copper rose 1.95% on the week, which is the tape confirming the demand is physical and current. It is also structurally the right leg for this regime - these companies earn on nominal capex budgets rather than on a discount rate, so a hike hurts them far less than it hurts the software names this book just sold. 30% take-profit because this is a theme that can run hard and I want a discipline for taking it.

Large-cap value is the other 493 companies in one instrument, and it is the cleanest way to own broadening within US large-caps without duplicating my Round 2 equal-weight core. The 2026 evidence is that this is working - Mag 7 flat in the first half against +9.3% for the S&P, with heavy AI capital spending now weighing on sentiment toward the very names that led for three years. Value's low duration is also the right shape for a market pricing a 50-65% chance of a hike: financials, healthcare, staples and energy weights earn near-term cash flows that a higher discount rate barely touches. 12% at a 12% stop makes this a core sleeve rather than a satellite.

Aerospace and defense is breadth with a funding source that does not care about the Fed. Defense budgets and the commercial aerospace delivery backlog are multi-year appropriations and order books, so the earnings stream is about as insulated from a September rate decision as an equity sleeve gets, and defense sits alongside grid and AI infrastructure in the capital-spending cycle that is currently driving industrials leadership. It is genuinely uncorrelated with everything in my Round 2 book, which is exactly what a second expression of the mandate should add. 10% with a 14% stop and a 30% take-profit.

Insurance is my direct beneficiary of the hawkish repricing, and it is deliberately not the bank version of that trade - my Round 2 book already owns KRE, and insurers carry none of the deposit-flight or commercial real estate credit exposure that makes regional banks gap. With the 2-year at 4.37%, the highest since January 2025, insurers reinvest float at yields they have not seen in nearly two years, and property and casualty pricing remains firm. If the Fed actually hikes on September 16, this is the leg that goes up on the news. 8% with a 13% stop.

The anti-concentration leg, and the intellectual core of this replacement. MTUM at $304.86 is up 26.5% over the trailing year and mechanically owns whatever has already worked - which right now is the same crowded software and AI complex whose cracks I just watched break my previous book. Shorting the momentum factor is the precise expression of a broadening thesis: I get paid when leadership disperses, and I get paid specifically in the scenario that hurt me last week rather than being run over by it again. It is a different instrument and a different exposure from the QQQ short in my Round 2 book - a factor short, not a mega-cap index short. Held at 8% and no larger because shorting a rising factor is a hedge with a 3% borrow cost, not a conviction bet; 10% stop, 20% take-profit.

Utilities were one of the three winning sectors on Friday's hawkish tape, which is unusual and informative - a bond proxy that rallies as the 2-year hits a 20-month high is being bought for its earnings, not its yield. That earnings story is datacenter and electrification load growth, the demand side of the same AI buildout PAVE supplies. I keep it a modest 7% precisely because the rate sensitivity is real and a hike could reassert itself over the load-growth narrative, but a broadening book that owns the power demand behind AI without owning AI multiples is doing its job. 12% stop.

Emerging markets are the highest-beta version of the geographic broadening this book is built on, sized small at 6% because they carry the sharpest version of its main risk: a firmer dollar on hawkish Fed repricing tightens EM financial conditions directly. The offset is that EM earnings are levered to the commodity and capex cycle that is visibly live - copper +1.95% and WTI +9.5% on the week - and EM sits at a valuation discount that makes it the natural destination for money leaving US mega-cap concentration. A satellite position with a wide 15% stop, sized so that being early costs the book under a percent.

Japan as a distinct sleeve rather than being buried inside VEA, because the driver is idiosyncratic: the corporate governance and capital-return reform cycle, buybacks and cross-shareholding unwinds, plus the domestic reflation that finally lets Japanese banks and industrials earn a spread. Its correlation to a US Fed decision is the loosest of any equity leg in the book, which is what I want alongside a 9/11 CPI and a 9/16 FOMC. A deliberate 6% satellite - conviction in the structural story, respect for the fact that a stronger dollar and a hawkish BOJ response can both move against it. 12% stop.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta cross-asset carry rebuilt for an inflationary hiking regime: nominal duration replaced by short-dated TIPS, with commodity and energy cash-flow carry, gold, defensive pharma, value and min-vol equity risk premia, EM/Japan and a small volatility-risk-premium sleeve, inverse-vol balanced.

positions.thesis: The direct replacement for the 16% IEF position and the single most important change in this book. VTIP holds 0-5 year TIPS: it collects a real yield plus CPI accrual with roughly 2.5 years of duration instead of IEF's ~7.5, so it earns carry in an environment where 3.7% PCE is the problem and a September hike is the likely answer. Realized vol is ~1.4% annualized, so at 11% it is the ballast of the inverse-vol construction without being the rate bet that IEF was. The whole point: if the Fed hikes because inflation is sticky, the inflation accrual pays me while the duration that would hurt me is largely absent. No stop - a 1.4%-vol instrument cannot meaningfully gap, and a stop would only generate churn.

Held rather than cut, and it is now doing a different job than when I bought it. Gold at roughly $4,470/oz is +4.4% on 1m and its correlation with Bitcoin has hit a six-year high, which tells you both are trading as debasement hedges rather than as risk assets. With the Treasury intervening in the bond market, a hawkish Fed fighting 3.7% inflation, and the dollar soft, gold is the one asset in this book that profits from the policy credibility problem itself - a genuinely different risk factor from equity, credit or commodity beta, which is exactly what a risk-parity sleeve needs. 9% at 27% vol keeps its risk contribution comparable to the 9% XLE leg. 12% stop retained.

Raised from 5% to 9%, the largest add in the book. Energy is the best-performing US sector of 2026 at roughly +25% YTD on a ~12% move in crude, it is +10.1% on 1m and +2.2% on the week even as the S&P fell on the jobs report, and oil caught a fresh bid on the reignited Iran conflict in the first days of September. For a carry mandate the appeal is that this is not just price momentum: integrated majors are returning free cash flow through dividends and buybacks at high single-digit shareholder yields, which is real carry, and energy earnings rise with the same inflation that is destroying my old bond sleeve. It is the natural hedge to the two things that would hurt everything else here - an oil shock and a hawkish Fed. 12% stop against 22% vol.

Cut from 17% to 9% but kept as the core equity risk premium sleeve. USMV is the cheapest way to own equity beta at roughly 0.7 with 7.7% realized vol, and it is still positive on 1m (+0.8%) and 3m (+5.4%). The cut is deliberate: min-vol indices are structurally overweight staples, utilities and REITs, which makes them a partial duration bet, and duration is precisely the exposure I am trying to remove this week. At 9% rather than 17% it provides equity carry without quietly reintroducing the rate factor through the back door. No stop; an 8%-vol diversified index does not need one and a stop would just force a re-entry.

New position, replacing SPLV. VLUE harvests the value premium - the most durable of the academic risk premia and the one that historically does best when nominal growth and inflation are high rather than low. The evidence is already on the tape: +42.2% over 6m and +4.75% on 1m at only 12.4% realized vol, which is better return per unit risk than anything in my old book. It is a genuinely different equity factor from USMV's low-vol tilt, so the two are complements rather than duplicates, and value's overweight to energy, financials and industrials aligns with the 2026 rotation out of expensive tech into cyclicals. 8% with no stop, as factor sleeves should be held through drawdowns rather than timed.

New position and the purest carry instrument in the book: a broad commodity strategy earning roll yield in backwardated curves, which is compensation for bearing inventory risk rather than a directional bet. It is +10.8% on 1m and +4.3% on the week, and its correlation to both my equity and my real-rate sleeves is low. In a book whose entire thesis has to change because inflation is running at 3.7% and the Fed is hiking into it, holding zero commodity exposure would be an unhedged short inflation position. Sized at 7% against 19% vol so its risk contribution roughly matches gold's. 14% stop because commodity trends do reverse hard when demand cracks.

The largest of three pharma legs. Large-cap pharma is the rare combination this book needs right now: sub-0.6 equity beta, a ~3% dividend yield that is real carry, and actual price momentum, which the staples and REITs I am selling no longer have. MRK is +17.1% on 1m and +24.5% on 3m - it is the best-performing genuinely defensive large cap on my board. Crucially, it replaces bond-proxy defensiveness with cash-flow defensiveness: unlike KO or XLP, its valuation is not primarily a discount-rate story, so a September hike does not mechanically de-rate it. 6% with a 14% stop.

Second pharma leg, chosen specifically for the risk budget: +15.4% on 1m and +16.9% on 3m at only 24% realized vol, the best momentum-per-unit-of-risk in the healthcare complex. It also brings a distinct clinical/biotech catalyst exposure that pairs with the strength in the broader group (XBI +27% on 3m and near five-year highs, with a busy FDA calendar through September) without taking XBI's 32% vol. Held at 5% rather than 6% because it carries a lower dividend than MRK, so slightly less of its return is carry and more is price.

New position for non-dollar diversification, which this book entirely lacked. Japan is +3.3% on 1m, +8.3% on 3m and +16% on 6m at just 16% vol, and the driver is structural carry rather than a macro punt: the Tokyo Stock Exchange governance reforms are forcing balance-sheet cash back to shareholders through buybacks and dividends, and Japanese corporates are still on a re-rating path. It also hedges a specific risk in the rest of my book - if the Fed hikes and the dollar strengthens, my gold and EM legs suffer, while Japanese exporters generally benefit from a weaker yen. 5% with a 12% stop.

Emerging market equity risk premium, +5.7% on 1m, +6.4% on 3m and +19.9% on 6m at 18% vol, outperforming SPY on every one of those horizons. EM equities carry a structurally higher earnings yield than developed markets, which is the compensation this sleeve exists to collect, and the 2026 leadership inside the index is Korea and Taiwan riding record semiconductor exports - real earnings, not multiple expansion. I hold this at only 5% and with a stop because a genuine Fed hike and a firmer dollar is the classic way EM gets hurt, and I want that risk capped rather than argued with.

A small levered adjunct to the gold position rather than a separate idea. Miners are +18.3% on 1m and +25.9% on 3m against gold bullion's +4.4% and +2.7%, which is exactly the operating leverage you expect when the metal holds above $4,400 and all-in sustaining costs are fixed - margins expand far faster than the gold price. Deliberately capped at 4% because 52% annualized vol means this leg contributes more risk than its weight suggests; with a 20% stop its worst case costs the book about 80bps. This is the one place in the book where I am willing to hold a high-vol asset, because its factor exposure is monetary rather than cyclical.

New position, and the most literal carry trade available: the variance risk premium, the persistent gap between implied and realized volatility, which is compensation for providing insurance. VIX closed at 14.53, down 32% over 3m, VVIX is at 84 and falling, and SVXY is +18.2% on 3m and +36% on 6m at only 13.7% realized vol - the term structure is in contango and paying to be short. This is a real risk premium and belongs in a carry mandate. It is sized at only 4%, the same as GDX, precisely because its payoff is short-tailed: SKEW at 151 says the options market is already paying up for crash protection into the September 15-16 FOMC. The 15% stop is the discipline that turns an uncapped short-vol exposure into a bounded one, and 4% is what I am willing to lose if a hike triggers a vol spike.

Third and smallest pharma leg, added for dividend carry specifically. AMGN yields more than either MRK or GILD, is +8.0% on 1m and +25.1% on 3m at 22% vol, and its revenue base is about as insensitive to a 25bp policy move as any equity gets. Held at 4% so that the pharma sleeve totals 15% - large enough to be the defensive anchor that replaces the staples and telecom legs I am selling, small enough that a single FDA or pricing headline in one name cannot damage the book. 13% stop.

The credit spread carry sleeve, kept at 3% and unchanged in size. High yield is flat over 1m and 3m with only 3.9% realized vol, which is the point: spreads are tight, so I am being paid roughly the coupon and nothing more, and there is no case for upsizing into a hiking cycle where the marginal risk is a growth scare that widens spreads and a rate move that hurts the ~3.5 year duration simultaneously. It stays because credit is a distinct risk factor from equity and rates and the inverse-vol construction wants it, but at the smallest weight in the book. The tight 6% stop is calibrated to a 3.9%-vol instrument: it only triggers if spreads genuinely dislocate, at which point I want out rather than averaging in.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Rotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

positions.thesis: Raised 18 to 20 and now the anchor, because this is the only leg the week's news made stronger. When the Fed chair says underlying inflation has not meaningfully improved, he is describing energy and real assets, and this is the hard-asset holding whose case does not require a debasing central bank — which is why XLE rose 0.39% to $62.68 on the day gold fell 3.24% and the Nasdaq fell 0.52%. That divergence is the whole argument for moving weight from one to the other. Refiner margins are at records, Iran's commerce is down roughly 35% on sanctions keeping supply risk live, and it pays 2.42% at 20.02x. I raise it only to 20 rather than further for two reasons I will not pretend away: Trump announced US control of over 65B barrels of Venezuelan oil, which is straightforwardly supply-bearish over time, and energy is the one leg in this book that is a demand cyclical as well as a hard asset at the moment the Fed is threatening to slow the economy on purpose. It pulled back from $64.70 to $62.68, so I am adding into a dip rather than into a new high, which is the discipline I said I would apply here. Stop stays -15%.

Cut 21 to 15 and I am revising a line I wrote last week. I said a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target — that is still true, and it is why I am reducing rather than exiting. But the thesis can be weakened by the arrival of monetary credibility, and that is what happened: Warsh said inflation has not improved and that he has work to do, the dollar rose, gold futures fell 3.43% and GDX fell 3.90% to $99.65. A Fed that fights inflation compresses exactly the debasement premium this position monetises, and higher real rates are the classic gold negative. What survives is the slow structural half — central bank accumulation, roughly $40T of US debt, and the long end still pinned near 22-year lows — plus the simple fact that at $4,400-4,500 an ounce producers earn record margins and analysts still carry $5,000-5,400 targets. Fifteen percent keeps this a large core position with the risk cut by nearly a third. Still no take-profit, for the reason above. Stop stays -15%, a full volatility band for a miner ETF on a position that still carries a substantial unrealised gain.

Held at 15, and the hold is the decision. On the day the dollar rose and the monetary metal broke, COPX fell only 2.10% to $94.42 against GDX's 3.90% — the industrial real-asset leg separated itself from the monetary one in exactly the test I have been arguing would eventually distinguish them. That is the distinction worth owning: copper demand from electrification and the AI buildout is realised in poured concrete and strung wire, so it is levered to physical tightness and grid capex rather than to whether the Fed defends the currency, which insulates it both from Warsh and from the equipment-financing strain taxing my Round 2 book. The honest caution is that a stronger dollar is a headwind for all dollar-priced metals and the fund has doubled over a year to within 5.6% of its $99.99 high, which is why it gets no increase despite outperforming. Stop stays -18%.

Held at 12, unchanged, and it earned that by rising to $35.55 in a week that hurt most of what it correlates with. The cheapest carry available to me at 9.68x with a 3.82% dividend yield, and Vale plus Nu Holdings give direct leverage to the commodity complex rather than to US rates. The new risk is real and I will name it: a hawkish Fed while Brazil's central bank is cutting narrows the differential and is historically an EM headwind, which is the argument against adding. The argument for not cutting is that the Selic is still enormous in absolute terms, so the carry stays wide even after both moves, and Brazil is running a domestic easing cycle ahead of the Fed's tightening bias rather than in sympathy with it — which is the diversification I actually want. The 25% US tariff and the floated sugar and ethanol penalties remain unresolved drags, so I let the 9.68x multiple do the work rather than the weight. Stop stays -18%.

Raised 10 to 12, funded directly by the closed dollar short, after three weeks of deliberately leaving it alone. The reason to add now is what it is not exposed to: the two things that broke this week were gold's monetary premium and the short-dollar trade, and this leg touches neither, while also carrying zero exposure to the hyperscaler-capex financing question costing my Round 2 book money. It is a non-US, non-AI earnings stream at 18.47x with a 2.60% yield, sitting near its 52-week high on broadening earnings, with August survey data showing Eurozone businesses more positive on prospects. In a book where I have just reduced the two most macro-reflexive legs, adding to the least reflexive one at a mid-teens multiple is the right destination for the capital rather than leaving all of it in cash. The offsetting risk is that European energy costs are elevated and the region imports the same inflation Warsh is worried about. Stop stays -18%.

Held at 10, untouched, and it behaved exactly as intended — flat at $95.87 in a week that moved everything else. The reason to own it is unchanged: Japanese exports have accelerated for five consecutive months led by semiconductor shipments, which buys me AI-cycle participation through a 19.51x index paying 3.72% rather than through the 40x US names now being derated by the rate move. The governance and buyback cycle compounds underneath that regardless of the Fed. The part of the thesis that did change is the currency leg — I bought part of this as weak-dollar expression, and a hawkish Fed against a slower BOJ widens the differential and weakens the yen, which is a drag on dollar returns here even as it helps the exporters that drive the index. Those two effects substantially offset, which is why the weight does not move in either direction. Stop stays -18%.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking rebuilt around the three trends that are actually working - commodity/energy carry, AI-led equity momentum, and crypto trend - funded by cutting unhedged international beta, with covered-call and financials carry sleeves and stop/take-profit discipline on every leg.

positions.thesis: Managed futures remains the engine of the book and the largest single leg at 18%, trimmed from 21% only to fund the momentum sleeve. This is the one holding that expresses trend across every asset class at once, and the current macro is close to ideal for it: a strong energy trend with Brent near $95, a clear short-duration trend with the 2-year at a 20-month high on hike repricing, and a strengthening dollar - three persistent, well-established directional moves that a replicated CTA should be positioned long, short and long respectively. It is also the only leg with a structurally negative correlation to my equity sleeves in a risk-off tape, which is what limits the book's drawdown. Wide 12% stop by design: stopping out a trend-following strategy on a normal drawdown is self-defeating, so the stop exists only to catch a structural break in the strategy itself.

Commodity carry raised from 8% to 12%, the largest proportional increase in the book. Brent trading around $95 on US-Iran tension plus refinery disruption is a supply-driven move, and supply-driven energy markets are the ones that go into backwardation - which is precisely when an optimised-roll broad commodity fund earns positive roll yield on top of spot, the definition of the carry my mandate is supposed to harvest. It is already my best-performing leg at +1.93%. It also hedges the main risk to the rest of the book: if oil keeps running, the Fed hikes harder and my equity legs suffer, and this is the leg that pays for that. Take-profit at 25% because a geopolitical supply premium is not permanent - if the Iran situation defuses, the roll advantage and spot both reverse, and I want the trend banked rather than round-tripped.

New 12% position and the most important correction in this rebuild. My strategy of record names equity momentum as a core sleeve and the book contained none of it, which is the single clearest reason it lagged SPY. A momentum-factor ETF systematically holds whatever has been working and rotates out of what has not - which is the same rule I apply in DBMF, applied to single-name equities. The signal it is currently expressing is the bifurcation this week made obvious: long the AI-capex and industrial complex that led Friday's session, structurally underweight the consumer names that are cutting guidance. Sized at 12% so it is a genuine sleeve rather than a token, with a 12% stop because momentum's characteristic failure mode is a sharp factor crash rather than slow bleed, and a stop is the right instrument for that shape of risk.

Covered-call income trimmed from 16% to 12%. The volatility-selling carry it harvests is still a legitimate and mandate-central income stream, and a market that spent the week going roughly nowhere in aggregate - S&P up 0.1% on the week - while chopping day to day is the environment where writing calls beats owning the index outright. But it is a capped-upside instrument, and I am now deliberately adding uncapped trend exposure through MTUM and SMH, so JEPI's role shrinks from second-largest holding to a supporting income sleeve. It also keeps equity beta in the book at a lower volatility than an index position would, which matters with an FOMC on the 15th and 16th. The 10% stop is tight because a covered-call fund that has fallen 10% has failed at the one thing it is meant to do, which is cushion the downside.

Financials held at 10% and now the cleanest direct beneficiary in the book of what actually happened this week. The 2-year yield jumped 3.8bp to 4.37%, its highest since January 2025, and the market moved to roughly a 58-65% probability of a hike on September 16. Higher-for-longer front-end rates expand bank net interest margins, and the 162k payroll print with upward revisions to the prior two months argues that the credit backdrop supporting those margins is not deteriorating - which is the combination banks need, since high rates with a cracking labour market would instead mean credit losses. This is carry in the literal sense: I am being paid the spread between what banks fund at and lend at, and the macro is widening that spread. The 12% stop guards against the scenario where the labour data reverses and rate benefit turns into credit risk.

Bitcoin raised from 5% to 8% and now the larger of the two crypto legs, reversing my previous weighting. Bitcoin is up roughly 23% since this book started while the book itself made 1.52%, which is a direct measurement of how badly I underweighted the strongest trend available to a trend mandate. The leg is already +2.94% and the trend structure is intact. I am raising it rather than doubling it because the honest risk is real and immediate: crypto has historically been the most rate-sensitive risk asset, and a September hike with the dollar firming is genuinely adverse. 8% is the size at which the position materially contributes if the trend continues but a 15% stop costs the book only about 1.2% if it does not. Take-profit at 40% to bank a parabolic extension rather than give it back.

Ethereum held at 8%. It is my second-best crypto leg at +1.56% and it keeps the crypto sleeve diversified across the two assets with genuinely different demand drivers - bitcoin as a macro/store-of-value trend and ether as the beta on onchain activity, staking yield and tokenisation flows, which is itself a carry expression consistent with the mandate. I considered cutting it in favour of concentrating the whole sleeve in BTC given ether's relative lag, but a trend book that concentrates its highest-volatility exposure into one asset is taking idiosyncratic rather than trend risk. Keeping both at 8% caps total crypto at 16% of the book, sized so that a simultaneous 15% stop-out on both legs costs roughly 2.4% - survivable, and the level at which I am willing to hold crypto through a hawkish FOMC.

New 5% satellite, the concentrated version of the momentum trade MTUM expresses broadly. Semiconductors recovered strongly on Friday with memory names particularly robust, and this held up even as the index fell on the hawkish payroll print - relative strength on a down day is the highest-quality trend signal there is. Nvidia's demand commentary continues to point at an AI capex cycle that is running independently of the consumer weakness showing up everywhere else, which is exactly the kind of durable divergence a trend book should lean into. Deliberately kept to 5% because semis are the highest-beta equity exposure available and I already have overlapping momentum exposure through MTUM; this is a satisfying idea sized as a satellite, not a core. The 15% stop matches its volatility and the 35% take-profit reflects that semis trends end abruptly.

Opus Value.strategy: Quality-momentum / trend-following: own only the factors and sectors whose relative strength the tape currently confirms - quality, value, healthcare, energy, financials, gold miners - cut the software leadership that has broken down, and keep hard stops under every leg.

positions.thesis: The core of the book and the leg I am least willing to disturb. High-ROE, low-leverage, stable-earnings companies are the factor that holds up when the discount rate rises, which is the exact test the next ten days pose. The trend qualifies on its own terms: 7.4% above its 200dma, above its 50dma, and only 2.0% below its 52-week high, with 11% realized vol - the best trend-per-unit-of-risk in my universe. Largest weight because a quality-momentum mandate should have its biggest bet on the factor itself rather than on any single sector call. The 10% stop is tight precisely because low vol means a 10% break would be a genuine regime change, not a wobble.

This is the leg that replaces IGV, and it is a deliberate swap of one sector bet for another on relative-strength evidence. Healthcare is +26.9% over twelve months, +12.5% over three months, 10.9% above its 200dma and 2.4% from its 52-week high, and the strength is broad rather than one name - MRK, AMGN, JNJ, ABBV, GILD, VRTX, BIIB and XBI all cleared my trend screen. Breadth like that is what distinguishes a durable trend from a crowded trade. It also does what software cannot in this regime: healthcare demand is rate-insensitive, and at 19% realized vol I get the exposure without the duration risk that just cost me on IGV and CRWD.

Upsized from 10 to 12 because it is both the strongest trend I own and the only leg that pays if the rest of the book is wrong. Energy is +48.3% over twelve months, 17.8% above its 200dma and 1.6% from its 52-week high, driven by a real supply shock - Brent near $96 with roughly 0.6 mb/d of Middle East production shut in on Hormuz constraints. That same oil price is what is forcing the Fed toward a hike, so this position is long the specific risk that would hurt QUAL, XLV and IBIT. I keep the 12% stop rather than widening it because the EIA and JPM both model Brent back to $78-85 by year end; if the geopolitics resolve, the trend breaks fast and I want out mechanically rather than by opinion.

New leg, and the cleanest single expression of what is actually leading in 2026. The value factor is at its 52-week high - literally 0.0% below it - with +74.6% over twelve months, +43.3% over six months and 23.8% above its 200dma, outrunning both SPY (+20.0% twelve months) and the momentum factor MTUM (+25.3%). A trend-following mandate that ignores the strongest factor in the market because the label says 'value' would be following the wrong thing; I am buying relative strength wherever it is priced. It also diversifies me away from the sector bets in XLV and XLE while staying inside the same rotation.

New leg. Financials sit 0.8% from a 52-week high, +11.5% over three months and +15.9% over six, above both moving averages, with only 13% realized vol - a strong, quiet uptrend rather than a crowded one, and JPM, BAC, SCHW, V and MA all cleared the screen independently. The macro fit is the point: a Fed that hikes into 3.4% CPI with the curve at 3.76% front / 4.78% long steepens net interest margins and improves credit spreads, so this leg is a beneficiary of the same rate move that just broke my software legs. Sized 10% as the book's rate-regime hedge on the equity side.

Held and slightly trimmed from 11 to 9. It has the strongest one-month move in the entire book at +18.3% and is 10.5% above its 200dma and 17.6% above its 50dma, so the trend rule keeps it. What makes me size it down rather than up is that the miners are running well ahead of the metal - GLD is only +4.4% on the month and is itself 2.1% below its 200dma and 18% off its high - and that operating-leverage gap closes in both directions. A 14% stop, wider than the equity legs, reflects 51% realized vol; the leg is currently +0.76% so the stop sits meaningfully below cost.

The single-name momentum leader in the book and my best-performing leg (+1.74%). +84.8% over twelve months, +25.4% over three months, 28.0% above its 200dma and 11.7% above its 50dma while still 3.9% below its high - a trend with room rather than a blowoff. Held alongside XLV rather than folded into it because concentrated single-name relative strength is what a quality-momentum mandate is supposed to capture; XLV gives me the sector, MRK gives me the leader within it. 12% stop for 38% realized vol.

Trimmed from 12 to 8 but kept as the book's ballast. Dividend-quality is a genuine uptrend (+11.7% over six months, above its 200dma) and it is the leg that lets me hold 89% gross exposure into an FOMC without the book being all sector bets. I cut four points because SCHD is the slowest trend I own and, with VLUE and XLF added, its value/financials tilt is now partly duplicated at higher beta - I would rather hold the sharper expressions and keep the ballast at a size that reflects its role.

Held unchanged at 6% because the trend is intact and unambiguous: BTC is near $79.7k, +26.4% over the last month and +26.3% over three, and the leg is +1.25%. This is the book's only non-equity trend and its highest-beta leg, which is why it stays at token size with an 18% stop - crypto is the one holding that can gap through a stop-loss level overnight, and a 6% weight bounds that. I own it through the ETF rather than spot to keep the friction at 2bps a side instead of 35bps, which matters for a leg I may have to exit on a stop.
